The matters within the Chan school clarify that beneath one's heels there is fundamentally no substantial dharma. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Do not think of good;
do not think of evil. Yantou said: "The time when one thinks of nothing at all is called the 'right word' (*zhengju*). If you wish to recognize this word, look toward the phenomenal reality.
To look for it is swift; to grope for it beneath the faculty of thought is slow.

Yet, within the application of the pivot, a slight glimpse is revealed—like a flash of lightning, like sparks struck from stone. Such swiftness is difficult to encounter; how could it allow for deliberation?

What is called "the livelihood of those who transcend" began with the Flower held aloft at Vulture Peak and the wall-gazing at Shaolin, reaching its full realization under Great Mirror (Dajian Huineng), whereby the Dharma pervaded the entire universe.
Thus it was. Subsequently, the five schools branched out from a single source; their gateways for transformative teaching flourished and declined in varying degrees.
For the salvation of those below, the Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasties relied upon the lineage of Tiger Hill (Hǔqiū), which has continued to spread down to the present day.

Yet, regarding the *Zhengfayan zang* and the *Zhiyuelu*, there has been no one to follow Xuedou’s selection. The recorded sayings and机缘 (ji-yuan) of various masters exist only as fragmented manuscripts and scattered volumes, gradually...

It has fallen into oblivion; later scholars have had no means to verify it. This single thread of transmission carries an especially heavy responsibility. Master Tai was originally of the Confucian scholarly class;

in his youth, he was steeped in the ancient classics. After passing the civil service examinations, however, he was driven by the winds and dust of worldly affairs, finding no benefit for himself or others.

Whenever he heard even a single word or half a verse of the *Sūtra*, he would immediately find resonance within his heart, leading him to mistakenly suspect that the Way of the One Vehicle [must exist].

The path may be traversed. Yet, by following false conditions to seek a way to achieve union with it, one becomes further ensnared in the hooks and chains of fame and profit, unable to extricate oneself.

Wandering aimlessly to the ends of the earth, with hair white and teeth fallen out, one reflects that the matter of birth and death is of great importance—its urgency like fire burning the eyebrows or skin being flayed, allowing for no delay.
Thereupon, one withdraws from view in a humble hermitage to provide for one’s own livelihood and closes the gate.

He secluded himself from visitors and applied himself with keen resolve to penetrate the ultimate depths. One day, while walking in meditation at a leisurely pace, he was triggered by Yuan Sha’s words regarding "standing on the spot" (*li-di*).
In a flash, he grasped the nostrils of his mother-birth; he stepped upon the local scenery of the original ground.

Overjoyed and leaping for gladness, he came to know with certainty that this Way is primordially manifest, not belonging to language, nor falling within the realm of cognition and views. Nevertheless, it pervades...

While perusing the recorded encounters (*yulu*) of the ancient worthies, I found that regarding their diverse pedagogical applications and the final, secure barrier, there remained much room for doubt.

Recently, while staying at a hermitage with the layman Xinyuan during the summer retreat, we took up the *Zhizhuyue lu* (Record of Pointing at the Moon) and the various lamp histories to extract the Dharma words and recorded encounters of the venerable masters from Yinyang onwards.
We examined each one individually, providing critical commentary and definitive resolution; only then did I come to understand the ancients.

The master’s skillful means in killing and enlivening were nothing other than a profound illumination of the matters transmitted from of old. Thereupon, my former doubts dissolved like melting ice, and the matter beneath my heels was seen through with no remainder. I privately rejoiced that in the twilight of my years, I had recognized the path home; from this point on, I returned home to sit in peace, and only now do my breaths settle. Looking back at my fellow practitioners, I see them as follows: [Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The following is a continuation of the thought based on the context: ...I observe those who share my way. Some have attained the Way but have not yet returned home; some have returned home but have not yet settled in their sitting; and some have neither attained nor returned. Alas, how many are there among us who, having attained the Way, have yet to return home? How many are there who, having returned home, have yet to settle in their sitting? And how many are there who have neither attained nor returned? May we all, by the grace of the Buddhas and patriarchs, attain the Way, return home, and settle in our sitting, so that we may truly be called disciples of the Buddha. Thus I speak. May you all take heed. Some are submerged in jars of pickled vegetables; others stumble upon forked paths. Their search for the mind remains unceasing, making their journey uniquely arduous—precisely as it was in the past at the Terrace (Tiantai).
This is what is meant by the saying: "Having once been a profligate, one feels particular compassion for the traveler.
This flickering, single-minded resolve cannot be restrained; this is why the *Black Bean Collection* (*Heidouji*) was compiled. It traces back, in fact, to the Patriarch Ying’an Hua.
The legacy of Tiger Hill vibrates on, stretching far without interruption; it flourished once more at Longchi.

During this time, dragons and elephants trod upon the earth, following such venerable masters as Miyun, Tianyi, Xueqiao, and Zhanran. The Master’s roar was like a forest, with great bells resounding in succession.
Reaching Yangxi, the myriad streams returned to the abyss; the thousand peaks reached the sacred mountain. How magnificent and vast! Great indeed is Guan!
Stop! Yet, when the scroll is unrolled, the eyes are bewildered by the five colors. Great men of immeasurable capacity have had their very eyes replaced by black beans;
those of lesser caliber merely engage in circular speculation, wandering further and further from the truth as they search.

In this world, there are those of spiritual roots and wise nature who, were they willing to take up the burden upon one shoulder before the black bean has even sprouted a shoot, would be able to seize it.
A single blade of grass manifests as a sixteen-foot golden body; taking up that sixteen-foot golden body, he treats it as a single blade of grass.
With a cough, a spittle, or a wave of his arm, he brings about life and death without touching the edge of the blade, never falling into deliberation.

This is the first stage of radiance before an ancient mirror has been polished—a light possessed by every person beneath their own feet. Those of long-standing practice and superior capacity may purchase this stone with ease.
Yun: At the initial stage of entering the Way, one carries the spring and attains the moon, hoping to be able to perpetuate and glorify the ancestral seat and shoulder the burden of the True Lineage.
Thus, the single thread of transmission from the West shall never fall into ruin.

Furthermore, the establishment of the Five Houses and the intent that "a thousand waves surge together beneath a single expanse of clear sky"—is this not to treat Mañjuśrī as equal to Samantabhadra? Alas! The Tathāgata...
For the sake of the one great cause, he appeared in the world. This was a separate transmission outside the teachings, where the path of words and language is severed.
Those of dull faculties suffer from the blindness of having no way forward;

yet gentlemen fortunate enough to possess the conditions for both merit and wisdom can extricate themselves from the five desires and seek liberation from saṃsāra. Furthermore, because of the dense forest of false views, they undergo suffering in vain.

I have labored tirelessly for many days, yet found no respite. You have bestowed upon me this volume; it is truly like a gourd-buoy in midstream, or an *utpala* flower blooming after a thousand years.
This serves as the preface.
Written by the lay practitioner Ping Shengtai on a summer day in the Jiayin year (1794), the 59th year of the Qianlong era.
Four Discourses from the Writing Brush:
Tiaoxi said: "I have a great illness that cannot be cured by the physicians of this world; Śākyamuni, the King of Physicians, is my healer. Mañjuśrī is the physician who attends to my physical form."
Furthermore, from the successive patriarchs of past dynasties down to the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of both ancient and modern times, all have been masters who heal the state.
Yet, while it is permissible for them to heal themselves, they cannot heal others. Thus it is said: "I have a great illness, which is not what the world can heal.

Moreover, since it is not something the world can heal, those who claim to be healers are themselves the patients. Since they cannot heal themselves, how could they heal others? Therefore, regardless of...

Words and phrases are illnesses. Raising an eyebrow or blinking an eye is also an illness. Raising a fist or brandishing a whisk is also an illness. Administering a staff or shouting "Ho! is also an illness.
Since all these are illnesses, can the physician be dispensed with? To dispense with the physician is to treat only one's own illness (a rotten seed, a scorched sprout).

Not to dispense with the physician is to treat the illnesses of all sentient beings (seeking through sound, seeing through form). Furthermore, if the physician were dispensed with, one would treat one's own illness first and only then attend to sentient beings.
As for illness: if one does not cease medical practice, then the physician does not fall ill. Yet among sentient beings, some are ill and some are not;

and while sentient beings are thus divided between being ill and not being ill, the physician nevertheless falls ill. It must be that only when all sentient beings are neither ill nor not ill does the physician then not fall ill.
To speak of it in descending terms, illnesses are equal. There is the illness of having already fallen ill, and there is the illness of benefiting through illness. Why?
This refers to the "illness that aggravates illness": it is to strike and penetrate toward the point before the movement has even been initiated.
What is meant by the "illness that benefits the illness"? It is to grope and search about step by step after the movement has already been initiated.
As for taking the medicine before the movement is initiated, I cannot describe its taste; one who recovers knows it for themselves. Having taken [the medicine] after...
To cite the "subsequent medicine" is like the salt that seasons food or the sauce that suits the palate; salt is for the rice, and sauce is for the drink.
How far removed is this from arsenic or hemlock? Ultimately, it is not the fault of the physician.
Thus, although sentient beings may be ill or healthy, the physician remains entirely free from illness. That the physician is not ill while I am ill—this is my conviction. (From *Tiāoxī Yī*)
[This] discourse is truly a skilled physician for chronic illness. [The Master] makes a *mudrā* (circle) and says: "The above is the offering of the illness. [Signed] Xinyuan.
In our school, there is only the breaking of dharmas; there is no establishing of dharmas. To break the house and scatter the dwelling is itself the making of a livelihood.
Formerly, when Nanquan was staying in a hermitage, a monk arrived at the hut. Nanquan said, "I am going up the mountain to do some work. Wait until mealtime; I will prepare the rice myself."
[The master] said, "I have eaten. Send one portion up here. The monk ate the rice himself, then suddenly smashed all his belongings and lay down on the bed.
Nanquan waited for him to emerge, but when he did not see him come out, he returned to his hut. Seeing the monk lying there, Nanquan also lay down beside him.
The monk then got up and left. Gentlemen, do you recognize this monk who ate Nanquan’s rice without failing Nanquan?
Is there any function here? Do you see how this monk sent a portion of excellent rice to Nanquan?

When Nanquan reached his mouth, did he swallow it immediately? It is like the World-Honored One appearing in the world for forty-nine years, tearing down a house—tearing apart the beams, the rafters, the pillars, and the foundations—until it is reduced to a single expanse of white ground;
thereafter, each of the rafters, beams, pillars, and foundations [stands revealed].
Rigorous and solemn. Thus, when Nanquan saw him, he immediately certified him, saying: "Since you are thus, I am also thus. An ancient said:
"If there were even a single dharma that surpassed nirvana, I would say it is likewise like a dream or an illusion.
Only when a student of the Way possesses such an eye can they properly examine the teachings and discern the heterodox from the orthodox in all quarters; otherwise, wherever they go—
Falling into pits and ditches, wearing shackles and chains, there is not yet a day when one can emerge from them.

Nanquan said, "This is driven by the power of the wind; in the end, it will surely crumble and perish. This old man’s eye of wisdom observed events of a thousand ages as clearly as an *āmra* fruit in the palm of his hand.
Now, there are those whose holes have been plugged with wedges; the skillful craftsman then uses a wedge [to remove the wedge].
He removes it; yet, having removed that wedge, he takes the very wedge used for its removal and treats it as a supreme treasure.
Consequently, once that wedge is removed, this wedge immediately becomes firmly stuck in the hole. He tries to remove another wedge, only to find another wedge filling the space;
thus it continues in succession through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, yet the wedges never end and the hole is never cleared. Furthermore:
In its most extreme form, before the former wedge has been removed, this wedge is thrust in; wedges and wedges stand side by side until no further cavities remain.

Yet there are those of wit who, having seen the wedge removed, immediately create another cavity, perhaps by blowing once or brushing once, establishing a cavity within a cavity—this is yet another wedge. Alas!
The great essentials of the Buddha-dharma can be summarized in a single phrase: "Do not defecate upon the pure ground. An ancient worthy said:

"Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; however, defilement must not be permitted. Merely manifesting patterns and colors constitutes defilement—this refers to the view of a Buddha and the view of dharmas.
To the left, one descends into the Iron Ring Mountains; as soon as one is born, one begins to gnaw. Spontaneously there is nothing to do; spontaneously one is stark naked.
This is precisely the swift attainment of resonance through conditions. Although the mind is thus perfect when speaking in this way, one has already defecated all over the ground.
Who else could have defecated it? A clever student who casts a single eye here will see when others speak.
Chan speaks of the Way; he speaks of the subtle and the primordial. He strikes one right in the mouth, intending to make him shut his anus.
Yet, there remains a trace of breath. Suddenly, a wicked dog-like servant comes forth—one who bites at the wooden stake of human excrement—and says:
"Although you do not manifest through words, nor do you cling to wordlessness, your mind is perfectly round. At this, [the Master] becomes unconsciously enraged and leaps down.
Zhen-chuang: Seize this slave! Ask him what he has to say; speak quickly, speak quickly! His eyes flicker and move;
I brandish the vajra-fist and shatter the head of this māra-son into fine dust like motes of sand. Tut!
I happened to read the *Fuzi Yuanliu* (The Genealogy of the Whisk), which cites these few words; this is the general purport of my brushwork here.

Layman [Xuyun], you have selected these texts to form a collection that serves as a bridge for future generations to study the Buddha-way. It is enough simply to cause every person who reads your collection to become a Buddha or a Patriarch;
it is not necessary for everyone to become a Chanting Master. In this way, you will not fail to repay the expectations of the Layman.
This is the intention behind the selection and carving of this volume by Shi Yifan. This is my humble view, which I present to you, the officials.
When the book is completed in the future, it may serve as a colophon, or it may serve as a preface—so be it. Written by Yuandun.

From the *Anthology of Black Beans* (*Ān-hēi-dòu jí*), Volume One:
Verses on the Words and Phrases Used by Buddhas and Patriarchs as Occasions for Awakening.

The World-Honored One ascended the seat three times. (The first instance is universal; the second is poison; the third is urgent. The establishment of the school’s gate and the profound discourse on entering into principle are all fully contained herein. Ultimately, the Dharma King has not a single [thing].)

The title is "Increasing Benefit for People. The verse says: "The mind is as it is; the realm is as it is. Head straight, tail straight. Not understanding how to discuss the Origin, One can only recognize the illness. This Dharma is without speech; This speech has no end. Before the mallet has been struck, The True King of Dharma’s correct command:

The Unconditioned True Buddha truly resides within my own body. [The Master] picks up the staff and says: "The brilliant and numinous is not me. Brightness, darkness, form, and emptiness are not me. Walls, fences, tiles, and pebbles are not me.

Earthworms and frogs are not me. Where am I? *Du!* (A sharp exclamation). The Goose King chooses his milk; he is by nature not of the duck kind. Do you wish to recognize his face? Three times he calls, three times he responds. When the hawk flies to Silla, there is neither call nor response—this is a dream seen on a donkey-year. Therefore it is said:"

In this very matter, if there were no spring breeze, the flowers would not bloom; yet when the flowers bloom, the wind blows them down. As for that one phrase regarding the ground where neither Yin nor Yang prevails—how will you speak it? [The Master] suddenly lets out a shout. He then offers this verse: When the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he was caught in a moment of dullness.

Three times he called, three times she responded; drums were beaten and bells were shaken. The Unconditioned True Buddha is like a turtle being proven to be a soft-shelled creature. Truly within my own body is the pupil of the eye.

*Ei!* One does not know, while the other knows. The Vajra-god rubs the back of a clay figure. Subhūti sat in meditative seclusion in the mountain cave, yet he beheld my Dharma-body. [The Master] comments: "The Bhikṣuṇī has deceived all the people in the world, yet she could not deceive the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One...

The Honored One has deceived everyone under heaven; he has deceived the bhikṣuṇīs, yet he could not deceive Subhūti. But tell me, where does the point of profit or loss lie? The verse says: Dharmakāya, Dharmakāya! A little rice and no firewood.

Oil, salt, soy sauce, and vinegar— In the eastern house and the western neighbor’s. A sheep’s head hangs on the rack; Dog meat lies across the block. Three pieces at eight *liang* each— Originally they were but half a *jin*. I showed them pearls, yet they knew nothing at all.

At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions all realized the Way for themselves. (Setting aside for a moment the realization of the Way by the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions, how will you all realize it now, with your very faces before you? Have you not heard it said?)

Eagerly gazing at the white waves, he lost his oar. [The Master] picked it up and said: "It cannot be realized upon the flower; it cannot be realized upon the whisk; it cannot be realized upon the fist; it cannot be realized upon the finger.

It cannot be realized even upon a blade of grass or a tree, a brick or a tile, a rooster or a dog, a worm or a frog. It cannot be realized even upon a mote of dust or the great earth, a moment of time or empty space, sages, immortals, Buddhas, demons, outsiders, sentient beings, hell or heaven, a jade palace or a Buddhist temple, or even a wine shop."

A brothel. Running a butcher shop or a peddler’s stall; eating and wearing clothes; lifting a foot or taking a step—none of these can be "offered" (薦). If you could offer them, what else would there be to do? If you are willing to offer them, it is a dream that has awakened. If you wish to offer them, it is precisely while dreaming that you should do so.

The verse says: Māras cannot spy upon it; Buddhas cannot see it. A palm cannot hold it; a chamber has never contained it. Consciousness cannot know it; the eyes cannot blink at it. The realms cannot store it; the world cannot alter it. It is not the dharma of ordinary beings, nor is it the Mahāyāna.

It is not the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra; it is not a scroll of the Avataṃsaka; it is not a great mass of fire; it is not a diamond sword; it is not the seal of the patriarchs; it is not the fan of the immortals. From the beginning there has been no transmission, and no one has ever recommended it. Sweep it away to return to the source; eradicate all expedient means. Where words and thoughts are cut off, not even a single thread passes through.

Rest immediately, and at that very moment, it is accomplished. I show you, student, the true face of Mount Lu. (When Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to turn the Wheel of Dharma once more, [the Master] held up his whisk and said: (Note: This refers to the famous dialogue between Mañjuśrī and Śākyamuni Buddha regarding the turning of the Dharma wheel.)

If you speak, you cannot turn him; if you do not speak, you cannot turn him. Even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear, their mouths like flowing rivers, they still could not turn him. Furthermore, even if every mountain, river, earth, grass, tree, and forest were each transformed into a subtle and wondrous eloquent mouth, they still could not turn him.

Do you understand? This is not turning the Wheel of Dharma; it is entirely the Dharma turning the wheel. If you say that I have entered parinirvāṇa, or if you say that I have not entered parinirvāṇa—[you are wrong,] O Ācārya.

Do not take offense with this old monk. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are the law of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing are extinguished, there is tranquil extinction (*śānti*).

For the sake of bliss. (He held up the whisk and said: "There is no cessation where birth-and-death does not arise; there is no cessation where who could extinguish birth-and-death? In the spring of the Jiyou year, he again summoned the Master to preach the Dharma, providing a vegetarian feast for him below Wencheng Tower and personally engaging him in consultation. Upon his departure, the Emperor bestowed white silver from the Inner Treasury as a gift.

In the autumn of the Gengxu year, the Emperor, considering that the manifestations of ghosts and spirits are subtle and difficult to fathom, summoned the Master—who was among the monks most extensively versed in the Tripitaka—to question him.
The Master, along with Mengtang E, Xingzhong Ren, and others, responded to the imperial summons and arrived at the capital, where they were housed at Dajianjiesi Temple.

The Master drew upon the sutras and cited the treatises to compose a work intended for presentation to the throne. Suddenly, he manifested slight illness. After four days had passed, he bathed, changed his robes, and took up his brush to write this verse:

Question: "The Śrāvaka’s seeing of nature is like seeing the moon at night; the Bodhisattva’s seeing of nature is like seeing the sun by day. How is it for the Master to see nature? The Master said: "The Yellow River has nine bends, yet its water originates from Kunlun. [The questioner] said: "This directly points to the human mind. The Master said: "It does not. [The questioner] asked: "Why not? The Master said: "Because it is not the ultimate. [The questioner] asked: "What is the ultimate? The Master said: "The ultimate is the direct pointing to the human mind. [The questioner] asked: "How is this direct pointing to the human mind? The Master said: "It is like the moon reflected in water. [The questioner] asked: "Is there any difference between the moon in the sky and the moon in the water? The Master said: "There is no difference. [The questioner] asked: "If there is no difference, why do they appear as two? The Master said: "Because the one is the source and the other is the reflection. [The questioner] asked: "What is the source? The Master said: "The source is the mind. [The questioner] asked: "What is the reflection? The Master said: "The reflection is the phenomena. [The questioner] asked: "If the source is the mind, why do phenomena arise? The Master said: "Phenomena arise because the mind is deluded. [The questioner] asked: "If phenomena arise because the mind is deluded, how can one return to the source? The Master said: "Return to the source by ceasing delusion. [The questioner] asked: "How does one cease delusion? The Master said: "Cease delusion by realizing that the mind is originally empty. [The questioner] asked: "If the mind is originally empty, what is it that sees? The Master said: "Seeing is itself empty; emptiness is itself seeing. [The questioner] asked: "If seeing is empty, how can one see the Buddha-nature? The Master said: "To see the Buddha-nature is to see that seeing is empty and emptiness is seeing. [The questioner] asked: "If seeing is empty and emptiness is seeing, what is the function of this seeing? The Master said: "Its function is to illuminate all things without obstruction. [The questioner] asked: "If it illuminates all things without obstruction, is it not dualistic? The Master said: "It is not dualistic. It is like the sun shining upon the four seas—it is one and the same light. [The questioner] asked: "If it is one and the same light, why do people perceive it differently? The Master said: "Because their capacities differ. Those with clear eyes see clearly; those with clouded eyes see dimly. [The questioner] asked: "If their capacities differ, can they ever become equal? The Master said: "They can. By polishing the mirror of the mind, one may attain clarity. [The questioner] asked: "By what means is the mirror polished? The Master said: "By practicing the Way without interruption. [The questioner] asked: "What is the practice of the Way? The Master said: "The practice of the Way is simply to maintain the mind in its original state, free from fabrication. [The questioner] asked: "If one maintains the mind in its original state, free from fabrication, is there still birth and death? The Master said: "Birth and death are themselves the original state. There is no birth and death apart from the original state. [The questioner] asked: "If birth and death are the original state, why do sentient beings suffer? The Master said: "Sentient beings suffer because they are attached to the original state. If they were not attached, there would be no suffering. [The questioner] asked: "How can one be free from attachment? The Master said: "Be free from attachment by realizing that the original state is beyond words and thought. [The questioner] asked: "If the original state is beyond words and thought, how can one teach others? The Master said: "Teaching others is like pointing at the moon; one cannot grasp the moon by grasping at the finger. [The questioner] asked: "If one cannot grasp the moon by grasping at the finger, what is the finger? The Master said: "The finger is the teaching. [The questioner] asked: "If the finger is the teaching, what is the moon? The Master said: "The moon is the realization. [The questioner] asked: "If the moon is the realization, what is the difference between the finger and the moon? The Master said: "The finger is the means; the moon is the goal. Without the finger, one cannot reach the moon; without the goal, the finger is useless. [The questioner] asked: "If the finger is the means and the moon is the goal, can one reach the moon by following the finger? The Master said: "One can reach the moon by following the finger, provided one does not mistake the finger for the moon. [The questioner] asked: "If one mistakes the finger for the moon, what error is committed? The Master said: "The error is to cling to the finger and lose sight of the moon. This is why many practitioners remain stuck in the teachings and fail to realize the Way. [The questioner] asked: "If many practitioners remain stuck in the teachings, how can they be led to realization? The Master said: "They can be led to realization by a teacher who knows how to point directly to the mind, just as I have done here. [The questioner] asked: "What is the significance of your saying, 'The Yellow River has nine bends, yet its water originates from Kunlun'? The Master said: "The Yellow River represents the flow of the Dharma; Kunlun represents the source of the Dharma. Though the river flows through many bends, its origin remains unchanged. Thus, though the teachings manifest in various ways, their essence is one and the same. [The questioner] asked: "If the essence is one and the same, why do the teachings differ? The Master said: "The teachings differ according to the needs of the listeners. Just as the same water flows through different channels, the same Dharma manifests in different forms. [The questioner] asked: "If the same Dharma manifests in different forms, how can one discern the truth? The Master said: "Discern the truth by looking inward. Do not seek it outside yourself. The truth is within you, like the moon in the water. [The questioner] asked: "If the truth is within me, like the moon in the water, why do I not see it? The Master said: "Because you look outward. Turn your gaze inward, and you will see. [The questioner] asked: "How does one turn the gaze inward? The Master said: "Turn the gaze inward by ceasing to seek external objects. When the mind is still, the nature is revealed. [The questioner] asked: "When the mind is still, is there stillness? The Master said: "Stillness is not a thing. Stillness is the absence of movement. Movement is the absence of stillness. Both are empty. [The questioner] asked: "If both are empty, what is the ultimate reality? The Master said: "The ultimate reality is the emptiness of emptiness. It is beyond description and beyond conceptualization. [The questioner] asked: "If it is beyond description and beyond conceptualization, how can one speak of it? Yet, whether laughing, joking, scolding, or reviling; speaking coarse words or foul language that others could not endure; or engaging in unrestrained discourse without being requested;

At the West Plains by the water, there was the Chan Master Jingzhong Puzhuang of Daiman Monastery on Mount Jing in Hangzhou Prefecture, a native of the Yuan family of Xianju in Taizhou.
He received the tonsure under Zu’an at Tiantong Monastery, but after a long time, he did not find resonance there and departed to travel. He went to visit Liaotang at Tianning Monastery. Tang—
The questioner asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Tiantong. The questioner said, "Braving the rain and piercing the cold, what such desperate urgency do you have?

The Master said, "Precisely because the matter of birth and death is urgent. The questioner asked, "What is this matter of birth and death? The Master made a striking gesture with his sitting cloth (*zuoju*).
The Abbot said, "Dare you come here to pull at a tiger’s whiskers? Go to the Hall! One day, while in the meditation hall, the Abbot brought up the story of the cypress tree in the courtyard.
As the Master was about to open his mouth, the Abbot struck him across the face with his palm. From this, he attained awakening.
Initially, he took up residence at Beichen Monastery in Fuzhou; later, he moved to Yunju. He asked a newly arrived monk, "Tigers and wolves block the road here; thorns and brambles..."
[The Master] reached the heavens. When the monk arrived, [the Master] asked, "What urgent business brings you here? The monk replied, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master.
The Master said, "I shall not ask about the phrase you spoke upon entering the gate; but as for the straw sandals beneath your feet, where did you get them?

The monk hesitated, and the Master gave a shout. He then asked, "Where did you depart from yesterday? The monk replied, "Mount Lu. The Master said, "No need for further examination. The Master often conducted such examinations.
The monk said, "I have recently received an official document ordering that you must deal with the Senior Monk (Upādhyāya). The monk said, "I am no spy.
The Master said, "Even so, you must first undergo interrogation. The monk said, "Master, do not use your power to bully others. The Master extended his hand and said:
"Bring forth the official pass. The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him with his palm. Another monk said, "I have long heard that the Master possesses such a vital pivot of teaching.
The Master said, "This mountain monk has lost the advantage. A monk asked, "I have heard that the Master possesses the pivot of 'making arrangements' (dian)."
"Is it so? The Master gazed at him intently. The monk replied, "I have already overturned the meditation seat.
The Master asked, "Where are you from? The monk said, "Keep your eyes open! The Master remarked, "You are a spirit that clings to the grass and perches upon the trees.
While clearing away the weeds, a monk asked, "When will this patch of ground be weeded clean? The Master raised [his hand].
The hoe said, "I do not know what you, Venerable One, call this. The monk was speechless.
The Master threw down the hoe and said, "When will this patch of ground ever be cleared clean? Question: "Riding the tiger’s head, gathering the tiger’s tail—what about the matter in between?
The Master said, "He has attained freedom. [The questioner] said, "As for the ancient saying, 'I too play with it'—"
[The monk] said, "It does not come out. [The Master asked,] "What is the meaning? The Master said, "Entering the water, one sees a tall man. The monk requested further instruction.
The Master said, "In your own portion, what is lacking that you come to request instruction? As the monk was about to respond, the Master said, "The mouth of the alms bowl points toward the sky.
[The monk] said, "This belongs to the ancients. The Master said, "I use it most appropriately. [The monk] asked, "What is it?"

[The Master said: "A wondrous and extraordinary matter. The Master said, "A field of a thousand years has eight hundred owners. [The monk] said, "I, this student, do not understand. The Master said, "To this day it cannot be taken away;
it is left for the old farmer to plow. [The monk] asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "When the trees fall, the cliff rocks appear.
[The monk] asked, "As for what the former masters said—that there are carp on the mountain and duckweed in the bottom of the well—what is the meaning of this?"
[The Master] said, "If you see it and do not seize it, though you think of it, it will be a thousand miles away. Addressing the assembly, he said:

"When masters of our school are driven by necessity, their single word or half-sentence is nothing other than for the sake of the student—extracting nails and pulling out wedges, untying adhesions and removing bonds. It is like skillfully brandishing the Great Sword (Ta'a);
naturally, one does not injure one's own hand. Nowadays, those who occupy the seat of the teacher and instruct disciples merely memorize words and texts."
They embellish their speech and boast to those who come after, increasing their evil habits while remaining ignorant of the path from which they themselves emerged.

It is like wearing tattered rags while walking through a thicket of thorns; one cannot move with ease. At this point, the direct pointing school of Shaolin has fallen to the ground—how truly lamentable!
You who travel as pilgrims must each carry your own eyes; do not allow yourselves to fall into the nets of others.
There is no way to show one's head. It is just as the ancients said: "Having entered this gate, do not harbor intellectual understanding.

According to my own view, even if you were to suddenly forget all intellectual understanding, you would still be a layman outside the gate. To reach this point, you must be able to distinguish between the black and the white.
Take care! Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "When I was clearing the wilderness, I dug up the foundations of the Dharma Hall and found—"
"A single blunt axe. For a long time I have gathered you brothers together. If you can make use of it, I shall entrust it to you with both hands.
But if you cannot bear its weight, I have kept it all this while; why such a frantic haste?
It would be better to cast it onto a rubbish heap and let it be scorched by the sun and blown about by the wind. Suddenly he took up his staff, struck once, and said: "Whip up the iron!"
"Oxen plow the great earth. Who can plant crabapples at the bottom of a well? Ascending the hall, [the Master] cited Panshan’s instruction to the assembly:

"The moon of mind is solitary and full; its light swallows the ten thousand phenomena. The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist. When both light and objects are forgotten, what is it then?
Dongshan said, "When light and objects have not yet been forgotten, what is it then? The Master said, "These two venerable elders are playing with words."
The objects do not know their names; each is given twenty blows of the staff. If you do not see the Way, what bravery is there in seeing the righteous and failing to act upon it?
On the twenty-third day of the tenth month of the Guiwei year of the Yongle era, he passed away at Budong Xuan (The Immovable Pavilion).

His secular age was fifty-eight, and his monastic seniority was forty-five. After cremation, wherever the smoke and flames reached, *śarīra* relics appeared like strung pearls. He was interred in a stupa.

Paozhizhan went to the Paozhizhan Rock, where the Master instructed him to investigate the koan: "It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, it is not a thing.

enter right here! Then he clenched his fists and said, "The secure barrier is closed; speak of what is within the home."
[The Master] said: "Let us speak. But tell me, how do you understand this phrase: 'Neither opening nor closing'? He gathered his *saṃghāṭī* robe and descended from the seat.

(Even if it were so, it would not yet be called a full raising of the banner. He ascended the hall and said: "The Buddhas of the three periods have spoken thus; the patriarchs of successive generations have spoken thus;
the old monks of the world have spoken thus; and I, Songshan, also speak thus. If there were anyone who did not speak thus..."
"To one who speaks thus, I shall give thirty blows. If there is anyone who speaks in such a manner, I shall likewise give them thirty blows.
Why? [He] struck his staff and said: "Under the gate of Mount Song, the mandate does not travel in vain. Ascending the hall, he said: "At the beginning of the month is the first day;
the light gradually emerges. At the end of the month is the thirtieth day; where can the light be found? Even were it the aged Śākyamuni..."
Kāśyapa said, "If you can bring it forth, all matters are finished. Someone, if you can say it, come forward and speak!

The original radiance and auspicious signs were thus (as before, they could not be brought forth). Later, he traveled to Dengwu in Gusu, where he took delight in the way the mountains and waters coalesced;
he subsequently halted his staff there. Before long, the fourfold assembly gathered from all sides, and it became a great monastery named Sheng'en.
On the twenty-ninth day of the first month of the Xinyou year of the Hongwu era of the Ming dynasty, he assembled the multitude and said: "The time for this old monk has arrived. Immediately—
He spoke in verse: "Seventy-nine years, a single flavor that clears the field of weeds; letting go with hands cast over a precipice, the bright sun shines in the sky.
Having finished speaking, he passed away peacefully. His entire body was enshrined on a ridge to the west of the monastery; the stupa was named Yongguang (Eternal Light).
His worldly age was seventy-nine, and his monastic seniority was sixty.
Song Lian was a native of Jinhu. His mother dreamed of a strange monk who was transcribing the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* by hand.
The monk said to her, "I am Yongming Yanshou; I wish to borrow a room to complete this volume. Upon waking, Lian was born, and for this reason he was named Shou (Longevity).

Later, his name was changed to Lian, with the style name Jinglian, and he took the pen-name Wuxiang Jushi (The Non-Phenomenal Layman). At six years of age, he could memorize over two thousand words a day;
at nine, he was able to compose poetry. He entered Mount Qingluo, where he read the Tripitaka three times. He once went to pay his respects to Qianyan Yuanchang.
He spoke at length with words like rolling thunder. The scholar wished to humble him and engaged in debate with him for several thousand words, but failing to reach a consensus, he withdrew.
Two years later, he visited the Master again. The Master said, "I have heard that you have read through the entire Tripitaka; is this true? He replied, "It is so.

The Master asked, "Have you read it with your ears, or have you observed it with your eyes? He replied, "I have both read it with my ears and observed it with my eyes. The Master said, "If the eyes were able to..."
The observer asked, "Who do you mean by 'you'? The scholar raised his eyebrows toward him, and they looked at one another and laughed.

He once also attended upon Chu-shih Qi, with whom he discussed the ultimate principle (*yuan*). Thereupon, he presented a compilation of his surplus remarks (*sheng-yu*) to seek correction; Qi praised them with great enthusiasm.
I entrust this to you; please protect and uphold it well. He once composed a eulogy for Yongming, saying: "I and the Teacher share a karmic affinity from past lives;
Within the light of Prajñā, there is no coming or going. Now beholding his remaining image, I prostrate again; Suddenly I realize the three periods of time are entirely like an illusion.
The single assembly on Vulture Peak remains as solemn as ever; May I realize the great, perfect wisdom of Suchness."
Chan Master Weian Deran of Songyin in Huating, Songjiang Prefecture, was the son of the Zhang family of that locality.
In his youth, he followed Wuyong Gui to receive the tonsure and traveled extensively to consult various masters, yet he found no point of realization.

Later, while in the assembly of Qianyan, he heard the master’s discourse from the high seat and attained sudden enlightenment. Shiwu Yongguo said to him, "Your karmic affinity lies in Huating. Thereupon—
He bestowed upon him the two characters "Songyin" (Pine Seclusion). Thereupon, he returned to his native village and built a residence on the southern slope of Guohui, naming it Songyin.

For three years, he did not step beyond its threshold. He once wrote out the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* using his own blood, which produced the miraculous phenomenon of celestial flowers filling the courtyard.
Moved by this, the local residents constructed a monastery for him. When Qianyan passed away, the assembly requested that he succeed him to the abbacy.

On the day of the assembly, a monk asked: "Having distanced yourself from the pines and waters, you have come to occupy this Dragon Peak. As the ocean-like multitude awaits at the dais, we pray that the Master will offer a benediction for the Emperor.
The Master said: "The Ten-Thousand-Year Pine stands upon Mount Zhurong. The monk said: "We have already received the Master’s instruction regarding the benediction for the Emperor;

as for the 'house style' of the successive patriarchs, what is it like? The Master said: "When winter arrives, Cold Food Festival is one hundred and five days away. The monk said: "Could this not be the Master acting as..."
[The monk] said, “There is no such place as a human dwelling. The Master said, “The axe-head is made of iron. [The monk] said, “If that is so, then there are no overnight guests at the Dragon Gate.
The Master said, “He has already been branded on the forehead. [The monk] said, “If one does not ascend the tower to look out, how can one know the depth of the vast ocean? The Master said, “...”.
"You say, 'How many hairs of eyebrows does this old monk have? [The student] said, 'A hall of wind and cold serenity; the meaning of a thousand ages is clear.
The Master said, 'You have missed it by no small measure. [The student] asked, 'I have heard an ancient saying: "The path that leads upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages.
Is this truly so, or not? The Master said, 'Where did you get that news? [The student] said, 'To sell gold, one must meet a buyer for gold.'"
The man asked, "Master, you just shouted; you said that 'though gold dust is precious, if it falls into the eye, it becomes a cataract.

What about this? The Master said, "You would do well to look at Lake Xiùhú; every night under the bright moon, golden ripples scatter across the water. The man said, "Thirty years from now, these words will spread far and wide.
The Master said, "These fabricated Chan followers are as numerous as hemp and millet. The man said, "May the assembly bear witness. This student prostrates."
[The disciple] bows. The Master then said: "The First Principle has already been smashed to pieces by Master Dongbai with a single blow of his mallet.
I cannot help but reveal a bit of news through the gateway of the Second Principle. For several years, I have twisted a rope made of tortoise hair;
today I shall take it up and bind the Buddhas of the three periods, the Seven Patriarchs of the Western Heaven, and the Two Ancestors of this land."
The nostrils of all the old monks in the world have been pierced through with a single string. Now tell me:
from where do the mountains, rivers, great earth, grasses, trees, thickets, the myriad phenomena of the forest, and all things sentient and insentient come? After a long silence, he said:
"Do not take your idle scholarly learning and bury it within the heart of the Patriarchs. He then cited San-sheng’s saying: "When I meet people, I do not go out; when I go out, I [meet them]."
“To act for others is to promote the Way; when I meet people, I come forth, yet once I have come forth, I do not act for them.
The Master said, “These two old fellows, though they enter and exit the same gate, are enemies from past lives. One lies on the peak of a solitary mountain, sleeping amidst the moon and clouds;
the other stands at the crossroads, raising dust and tossing soil. When examined closely, both are equally flawed.”
"Thirty blows for each of you. Now tell me, when Xinfeng holds up the staff in this manner, is he rewarding them or is he punishing them?
He suddenly picks up his staff, strikes it once on the ground, and says: "In the heavens, all stars bow toward the North;
in the world, no water flows but toward the East. Ascending the hall, he said: "The sun may grow cold, and the moon may grow hot, yet the demons cannot destroy the True Teaching."

As for the origin: there is no track or path. When the sixth month is blazing with heat, he scatters ice and snow; Mañjuśrī has nowhere to put his whole body, and Samantabhadra suddenly displays his ugliness and clumsiness.
Is this a true statement? Or is it not a true statement? If there were no idle matters hanging upon the mind, it would be a fine season in the human world.

Were it not for the skull being entirely dried up, How could one know the spring colors have risen upon the peach cheeks?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Set aside for a moment Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout. Everyone, bring forth a single phrase from beneath your own feet.
He drew a line with his staff and said: "Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon this long ago; until this very day, he has not attained the wondrous.
[He] instructed the physician: "One koan is the medicine of Jīvaka; the various sutras of the Great Canon are the compounding ingredients."
[This is] the method. Having brushed aside both paths, he laughs aloud; no need for acupuncture or moxibustion to rouse the *gāohuáng* (the incurable depths).

At the beginning of the Hongwu era, he was summoned on account of his Way. Before long, he returned due to illness. He once said: "Those who study the Dharma should not rely solely on their 'ground' (*jiàn-dì*) or their half-baked understanding.
Of what use can such things be? It depends entirely on how one practices. On the fourteenth day of the fourth month of the Wuchen year, he manifested [his passing].
[The Master] passed away in silence. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Songyin.
Chan Master Jukong Qibin of Mount Song in Henan Prefecture was the son of the Wang family of Hao County in Jin. He received the tonsure under Wuxiang of Chongxing Monastery.
In the *Bingshen* year of the Yongle era, he went to attend upon Ningran and requested instruction on the essentials of the mind. Ningran said: "You, toward..."
"Before Bodhidharma came from the West, try to utter a single word! The Master was at a loss for a reply and remained in doubt for a long time, unaware of the taste of food or drink.
One day, seeing a *huai* tree planted by the Qin dynasty, he suddenly attained enlightenment.
When Nanquan entered the Master’s chamber intending to present his understanding, he suddenly said, “Qibin has attained Chan. The Master then gave a shout. Nanquan asked, “What was that?
The Master replied, “How can you, Master, falsely accuse an innocent man? From then on, Nanquan subjected himself to even greater refinement; day by day he grew new and bright.
One day, Nanquan asked, “In the case of Zhaozhou’s exposure of the old woman, where exactly did the woman’s failure lie?”
The Master said, “A pair of iron hammers with no holes. [The student] asked, “What about Zhaozhou’s meaning?
The Master said, “Amidst a thicket of brambles, one adds further pits and traps. [The student] asked, “Shitou said, ‘Neither books reach him, nor does correspondence pass.
What is the purport of this? The Master said, “The same breeze blows over a thousand miles. [The student] asked, “As for Qingyuan’s lowering of his feet, what was that? The Master said, “Calamity.”

"A matter of disaster! (To pluck a flower is a failure; to dangle one's feet is a calamity. When the Dragon Girl offered her pearl, it was not worth a single coin. A man of noble spirit is like a king; how could he willingly allow himself to be treated with such dull indifference?
Nevertheless, he nodded his head and said: 'The One School of the Dongshan lineage rests upon your person.'"
The twenty-sixth generation descendant of the Sixth Patriarch,
Chan Master Baozang Puchi of Dengwei in Suzhou, studied under Master Wanfeng Wei and attained thorough realization of the Great Dharma.
Weifeng entrusted him with a verse, saying: "Great Fú’s ribs ache as he clenches his fists; the Three Essentials and Three Principles cut off both the orthodox and the biased.
A lion cub from the lair of Linji—lamp after lamp, the flame continues, transmitted through ancient and modern times. When Feng was about to enter extinction, someone asked:
"In the Master’s assembly, how many disciples have attained the Dharma? Feng showed them this verse: "Compassion without thought, flowers..."

The fruit ripens as the opening [of realization]; the ground is clearly manifest. With wisdom as the reality, he offered his earnest entrustment. Monk Huida came to pay his respects and fully recounted the origins of his awakening.
The Master rebuked him, saying, "The Buddha-dharma is like the great ocean; it becomes deeper the further one enters. How can you settle for staying right here?
One day, while Huida was standing in attendance in the meditation hall, the Master asked: "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way."

"How do you understand this? Tian asked as he stepped forward to inquire after the Master's health. He stood with his hands joined in *añjali*. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Having been here for all this time, you still hold such a view!
(A person must first deceive themselves; only then will others deceive them. And even when others deceive them, it is because they have already deceived themselves.
Tian then roused himself to intense study. On the second night, he suddenly attained thorough realization. He composed a verse, which began: "With a single punch, I break through the Great..."
In the void, the traces of ten billion Sumeru mountains are not revealed. I ask: who is the master within this? A single red orb surges forth from the Fusang tree.
[Zhixian] presented himself before the Abbot. The Master looked at him and smiled, saying, "Even though it is so, you must still protect and maintain yourself well.
When the time arrives, the principle will manifest of itself. Having received the entrustment, Zhixian took his leave; the Master saw him off with a verse. He then resided there.
The Mountain. A verse says: "To see with clarity is not Chan; advance further from the tip of the pole beyond the reach of words.
To propagate the ancestral way, my own principle: enter the mountains again for twenty years."

The lay practitioner Tian Suan of Suyang was by birth a renowned clan from Jiangdu. Having failed repeatedly in his examinations as a student of the imperial academy, he resolved to devote himself single-mindedly to the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
He applied himself with fierce vigor to investigation and study. At that time, the Governor He Mimian was propagating the Way in the southeastern region.
The Master was a preeminent disciple who had entered the inner sanctum. After he had been refined by the Master’s hammering for a long time, the heart-seal was suddenly entrusted to him.
The Master then took up a bamboo whisk and examined the monks; among those who came from all quarters to study, there were none who did not look up to Suanan as a living ancient Buddha.

Throughout the nation, he was called "Great Being Tian" rather than by his personal name. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Lately, those who are earnestly devoted to Chan practice are few. As soon as [the question] is raised..."

As soon as one encounters this *huatou*, one is immediately bound by the two demons of dullness and agitation. Little do they realize that dullness and agitation are precisely the opposites of the state of doubt (*yiqing*).
When the power of faith is deep, the power of doubt will necessarily be deep; when the power of doubt is deep, dullness and agitation naturally vanish.
As the Buddha told the assembly: "The great ocean does not harbor corpses; empty space is not stained by the five colors; a mass of fire does not conceal mosquitoes."
Within the dharma of non-abiding, there is no establishment of delusion or enlightenment. Those who nowadays practice Zen take the gateway of shadows and lights and cover themselves with it;
they enter hell as swiftly as an arrow shot. While a monk was reciting a sutra, a layman asked him, "What sutra are you reciting?
The monk replied, "The Lotus Sutra. The layman said, "Of its sixty thousand characters, which character has eyes? The monk was at a loss for an answer. The layman then struck him.
A monk entered the gate; the Master immediately bowed and shouted, "Walk fast! The monk bowed again, and the Master said, "What bowl are you looking for?
The monk shouted, and the Master struck him with his palm (Master Gao-tíng once practiced this command). The Master lived in a village of farmers outside the city, using his residence as a hermitage.
Monks from all directions came to visit him daily, crowding around his seat. One day, while he was conversing over tea with a group of Zen practitioners, suddenly—
He then cast down his bowl, joined his palms in farewell to the assembly, and passed away.

The twenty-seventh generation descendant of the Sixth Patriarch was Chan Master Dongming Xubai Huichan of Hangzhou Prefecture; he was the son of the Wang family of Chu. His father served as a tax collector in Danyang.
He became the administrative head (kē-sī) and settled there. From his youth, he was exceptionally intelligent. At the age of fourteen, he followed Miaojue Zhanran to receive instruction.
Once, while they were engaged in manual labor, Zhanran asked him, "What are you doing here? The Master replied, "I am slicing radishes. Zhanran said, "You only know how to slice radishes.
The Master replied, "I also know how to kill people. Zhanran extended his neck toward him. The Master said, "A surrendered general is not executed. Zhanran was struck with wonder.
Subsequently, Zhuan was appointed as the abbot of Shushan. Hearing that Weian was propagating the Way at Songyin, the Master intended to go and visit him.
Upon reaching a small hermitage, he made a vow, saying, "If I do not attain thorough realization on this journey, I shall certainly not return. He remained there for exactly six days.
Suddenly raising his head, he beheld the pines; at that moment, he attained sudden enlightenment. He then returned and sat in meditation day and night, as upright as an iron pillar.
Consequently, people of all quarters called him Chao Tie-ji (Iron-Back Chao). Later, he arrived at Dengwu in Gusu and visited Guolin.

Guolin instructed him to investigate Baozang’s case; his realization was recorded in the *Baozang Zhuan*. At Pingsantang on Mount Tianmu, he gathered companions and sat in meditation for a thousand days.
For a long time thereafter, he traveled to Gushishan in Anxi. Because the mountain peaks were so majestic and prominent, he resolved to spend the remainder of his life there.
He resided there for over thirty years, never venturing beyond the mountains. Monks from afar vied with one another to join him, and it became a great monastic complex.

In the year Yimao of the Xuande era, it was granted the imperial plaque of Dongming Chan Temple. Subsequently, he led the assembly in the reconstruction of the Great Hall of Jingci Temple. In the year Xinyou of the Zhengtong era—
On the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month, he suddenly gathered the assembly to express his gratitude and bid them farewell. When the assembly requested a verse, the Master said:

"The entire Canon of the Great Teaching—no one can look upon it; what use are these few idle words? At the hour of the Dragon on the twenty-ninth, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
His cremation yielded countless relics, which were enshrined in a stupa at the East Valley of Mount Ben. He was seventy years of age and fifty years since his ordination.
5. Chan Master Shaoqi Jingbi, known as Hansou of Chushan, was a native of Le clan from Andang in Shu. He was a resident of Tongchou in Anqing Prefecture.
In his youth, he received instruction from Yuanji Tong. He first went to consult Wujie; one day, upon hearing the sound of the wooden board, [he attained realization].
He had a realization. He further investigated the theme of "destroying emptiness," citing the phrase: "There are thieves who do not strike the poor house.
In the *Guihai* year of the Zhengtong era (1453), he again visited Wuji. Wuji asked, "Where have you been living for the past few years? The Master replied, "Vastly open and without fixed abode."
Wumen Ji said, "What have you attained? The Master said, "Originally there has been nothing lost; what is there to attain? Ji said, "This is something acquired through study.
The Master said, "Not a single dharma exists; from where could study come? Ji said, "Does this not fall into emptiness?"
The Master said, "I am not even 'I. Who falls and who is empty? Ji said, "Ultimately, what is the matter? The Master said, "The water falls and the rocks appear;

[Zhaozhou] said, "Although the Master holds fast at the vital ford, it is no small matter that you exhaust yourself. Jie [the attendant] struck his knee once. The Master then shouted.
Jie said, "One who can sustain the family must be one who can break the family; doing so to manage the household affairs is truly effortless.
The Master covered his ears and went out. That evening, he summoned the Master again and questioned him, saying, "Regarding the successive points of realization you have previously elucidated—"
"Speak it then," the Master said. Yunju replied from the truth. Yunju said, "Give me back the meaning of the word 'no'. The Master presented a verse, saying:
"The place where this monk asked was full of complications; How could Old Zhao ever have involved his thoughts?

A single word uttered spontaneously and fully revealed— Yet it turns out to be quite extraordinary, causing people to doubt. Yunju said, "What is your state of being without doubt? The Master said, "Green."
The mountains are green and the waters are clear; swallows chatter and orioles sing. Everything is distinct and vivid—what more could one doubt?
Jì said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master said, "The head touches the void; the feet tread upon solid ground. Jì then received his certification.
In the year of Renshen, he arrived at Jinling and visited Yuexi Haizhou. After he took up residence there, a monk asked, "What is the realm of Tianzhu? The Master said, "The mountain stream is wide."
The clouds return at evening; the mountain is high, so the sun rises late. [A monk] asked, "What is it like to be a person within this realm?
The Master said, "The brows beneath the forehead shade the eyes; the ears beside the cheeks reach the shoulders. [The monk] asked, "What is the家风 (house style) of Tianzhu?

The Master said, "Steam from cloud-like rice-pots cooks pine powder; an ice-cold cauldron brews moon-discs. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The sea..."
Shen scattered forth a night-bright pearl. [The monk] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Mañjuśrī has lost his glass cup.
[The monk] asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A cast-iron scale weight. [The monk] asked, "What is the Dharma? The Master said, "A stone or a clod of earth.
[The monk] asked, "What is the Sangha? The Master said, "A black-lacquered staff. In the year Yihai of the Jingtai era, he moved [to another monastery].

Touzi ascended the hall. A monk asked, "Having left Mount Xuan behind, you have come to occupy Touzi. With the assembly gathered before you, we pray that the Master will offer a blessing for the Emperor.

The Master said, "The long-life script within the cauldron; the ageless pine atop the peak. The monk said, "I have already received the Master’s direct instruction regarding the blessing for the Emperor.
As for the 'house style' of Touzi, what is it like? The Master said, "Passing through the marketplace carrying a pitcher is not selling oil."
The Old Man said, "It is just as the Patriarch said: 'I do not permit traveling at night; one must arrive by the break of dawn. Is this truly so?
The Master said, "Though there is sinew in his eyes, alas, his tongue has no bone. The Old Man said, "Zhaozhou said, 'I am already white as a monkey;
he is even blacker than a monkey. What was his meaning? The Master said, "Were it not for the exhaustion of the bow and arrow, he would not yet have raised his hand."

[The Master] lowered the banner. [A monk] asked, "Venerable Sir, today you ascended the seat to preach the Dharma; I wonder what auspicious signs there were? The Master said, "The qilin strides beyond the vermilion heavens;
the *utpala* flower blooms amidst the fierce flames. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "The snow melts and the mountain peak is revealed; the wind passes and the tree-tops sway. [The monk] asked, "When the precious sword has not yet emerged from its scabbard..."
The monk asked, "What is it like at that time? The Master said, "The spirits wail and the ghosts cry. The monk asked, "What is it like after it has been drawn from the case?
The Master said, "The Buddhas and Patriarchs swallow their voices. The monk asked, "What is it like when it has been drawn out and when it has not yet been drawn out?

The Master said, "A hairless lock of chain rattles at both ends. The monk lifted up his sitting cloth (zuoju). The Master then shouted. The monk hesitated; the Master struck him. He then said, "Scratching an itch on the head of a venomous snake."
To cast oneself into the mouth of a fierce tiger, one must indeed be such a person. That monk just now was much like a seasoned warrior, daring to come here to seize the drum and snatch the banner;
yet, alas, his head was a dragon while his tail was a snake, and he died beneath the staff.
Had he known how to turn back toward the path of life, he naturally would not have encountered the sharp edge of the blade. Therefore it is said: "To play with a snake..."

This is one who handles snakes; if he does not know how to handle them, the snake will bite and kill him. [He] ascends the hall, takes up his staff, and says: "This very thing is a source of confusion.
How many monks, upon reaching this point, find themselves unable to open their mouths, unable to conceive of it through thought, and unable to bring it forth.
Now it has fallen into the hands of this mountain monk. Whether held horizontally or vertically is up to me; I can even lift it up."
"Rising and putting down; rolling up and unfolding, killing and giving life—all depend on me. Pointing a single dot in the air with his staff, he said:
"At this very moment, from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old to the elder monks of the world, upon reaching here, they can do nothing but beg for their lives.
Is there anyone among you who can speak out on behalf of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? After a long silence, he struck the ground once with his staff.
He said, "The blind Vajra-Eye has been overturned, and the precious throne of the Empty King has been cast down. What kind of bowl are you all looking for? With that, he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, when the assembly had gathered, the Master adjusted his robes and took his seat. After a long silence, he said, "Everyone, take this clearly to heart.
With that, he descended from his seat. When the Master went to the garden and saw a winter melon, he asked the gardener, "This one has no mouth."
The head monk said, "Because I have never been idle for even a single moment. The Master said, "Does the master of the house still exert some effort on your behalf?
The head monk said, "I rely entirely upon his power. The Master said, "Bring him here to meet this old monk.
The head monk then prostrated himself. The Master said, "This is still merely a servant or a slave."
He turned his head and picked up a bamboo lash to strike the frame. The Master then laughed heartily and looked back at his attendant, saying, "There are insects in the vegetable garden.
The Head Seat Xingkong requested instruction on the Three Barriers of Mount Meng. He asked:
"When a gnat sucks dry the vast ocean, where do the fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs find a place to dwell and establish their lives? The Master replied: "On the road to Chang'an."
The Golden-Haired One lies down. [The student] says: "The Water-Mother flies up to the Ultimate Heaven (Akaniṣṭha) and enters the eye of Maheśvara to perform a dance.
Why is she not seen? The Master says: "Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion, the iron horses neigh. [The student] says: "The Lotus Lake Bridge points directly to all people.
Why does one with clear eyes fall into the well? The Master says: "The bright moon illuminates the traveler at night. [The student] says: "Please..."

The Master recited a verse. The Master said, "I would give you a severe beating for that. [The monk] said, "I am willing to accept the beating; I beg the Master not to be sparing with the verse. The Master laughed heartily and recited:
"When the occasion arises, he cuts off the passage between sage and ordinary; If one hesitates, one knows that his yielding has not yet been extended."
If you wish to know the ultimate meaning of Mount Meng, the hook is cast with the intent to catch the golden-scaled fish.

In the third month of the Gui-si year of the Chenghua era, the Master manifested slight illness. The assembly requested his final words. The Master extended both hands and said, "Do you understand? He spoke again:
"On this day this year, pushing a cart, I crash into a wall; I shatter the void, and a thunderbolt strikes the blue sky. Ha ha ha! The mud ox..."
He swallowed the pearl of the old dragon; the surging waves of the ocean of nature subsided. He passed away peacefully at the age of seventy, with sixty-one years of monastic seniority.
A stupa was erected at Tiānchéng.
The twenty-eighth generation descendant of the Sixth Patriarch, Chan Master Haizhou Puci of Dongming in Songzhou, was the son of the Qian family of Chanshu. He left home to become a monk at Poshan.
While reading the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*, he reached the passage stating that all verbal expressions are devoid of substantial meaning and cannot be found through investigation;

consequently, his appearance grew increasingly haggard. A layman asked him, "Master, you look ill. The Master replied, "It is simply because I do not yet understand the Buddha-dharma; it is not illness.
The layman said, "If you do not understand the Buddha-dharma, why not go to Mount Dengwu in the prefecture to seek instruction from Wanfeng Wei?"
"The Master is leaving. Hearing this, the teacher was delighted and went directly to Dengwu to see Wanfeng. Wanfeng asked, "Where have you come from, novice?
The teacher rose from his prostrations and said, "Changshu. Wanfeng asked, "What is your purpose in going there? The teacher recounted the previous conversation and bowed twice, seeking instruction.
Wanfeng then struck him twice on the head, gave him a kick across the back, and stamped him with both feet, saying, "This very thing is it!"
"Meaning. (The mouth is the gate of calamity). The Master had an awakening. He rose and said, "Excellent, excellent! You have expended great mental effort, Master.
Xuefeng smiled and granted him approval, bestowing upon him a verse that said: "The hair of a tortoise is entrusted to sons and grandsons; The horns of a hare are picked up to seek the ford."
"A single shout leaves one deaf for three days; who can truly be intimate with the message within? He further said, "You should conceal your traces to protect [the Dharma];
do not lightly act as a teacher or model for others. Believing he had attained this realization, the Master built a hut in a valley of Mount Dongting and remained there for twenty-nine years.
One day, a monk arrived, and the Master asked, "Where have you come from, Senior Monk? The monk replied, "Anxi."
[The Master] asked, "Is there anyone at Anxi? [The monk] replied, "Venerable Xubai is preaching the Dharma; he is no different from Gaofeng.

[The Master] asked, "Whose disciple is he? [The monk] replied, "Baozang. [The Master] asked, "What sayings does he have? The monk cited the words used by [Xubai] to test people in his quarters, saying:
"Mind is not Buddha; wisdom is not the Way; the Tripitaka is not the Dharma. What is it? Those who offered responses all failed to accord with the truth.
When he had finished speaking, he asked the Master, "Did you study under Baozang? The Master replied, "I studied under Wanfeng together with Baozang.
The monk asked, "What did you see on that day that led you to remain hidden here and never again go to study under another person? The Master said:
A monk asked, "There are only words here; there is no real meaning at all. Baofeng then struck him. The monk said, "I have attained awakening because of this.
The monk asked, "Please tell me the reason for your attainment. The Master said, "Simply that which knows pain and itch is the real meaning; it is the wondrous mind."
"Your words are merely skin and hair," the monk said with a laugh. "According to such a view, you have not yet resolved the matter of birth and death;
how can you claim to have attained awakening? It is not that awakening has not yet arrived—it has not yet arrived. Have you not seen it said: 'The mind is not the Buddha, and wisdom is not the Way'?
The Master then became doubtful and asked, "Is there anyone among that assembly who is truly and profoundly enlightened? The monk replied, "There is none. The Master immediately departed.

Anan crossed the lake to Anxi and went to visit Dongming. It happened that someone had prepared a vegetarian feast. When the Master arrived before the gate, he asked Dongming, "What is the flavor of today’s meal?
Dongming replied, "One knows it only when it reaches the mouth; once described, it is far removed. The Master said:
"What is it like to reach the flavor? Ming struck him down. Deng said, "If you recognize where the lamp-light falls, the flavor reaches your mouth.
(He was thus left baffled by him right before his face; how pitiable. The Master remained speechless. At dawn the following day, he sent an attendant to invite the Master.
The Master arrived immediately. Ming asked, "Have you seen anyone? The Master smiled and said, "I have seen only one person; I fear it would startle people if I were to speak of it.
Ming said, "Even if you had personally seen Śākyamuni, he would still be just an ordinary fellow.

What harm is there in speaking of it? The Master said, "Wanfeng. Ming asked, "Are you referring to chronological precedence, or to the Buddha-dharma? If you are referring to chronological precedence..."
“There are a thousand people beneath Mount Wanfeng. If we discuss the Buddha-dharma, you, old ācārya, have not even dreamed of it;
what is there to be startled by? If you had truly met Wanfeng, where would Wanfeng be right now?

The Master’s face turned red and he stood bewildered. (A person who knows shame is hard to find. Ming said, “If that is so, then you have never seen Wanfeng. The Master returned to his guest quarters. Three.
Day and night, he forgot both sleep and food. By chance, the cord of his incense burner snapped and fell to the ground; suddenly, he attained great enlightenment.
He went before the Barrier Gate to present the circumstances of his realization. Yuanming said, "Old *jiaoluo*, you shall receive the lineage of Wanfeng.

The Master replied, "Since you brought me to full penetration, how could I receive the lineage of Wanfeng? Yuanming then laughed. He subsequently gathered the assembly and emerged from the Barrier Gate, ascending the seat and saying: "Gautama..."
To whom was the intention transmitted? Kāśyapa broke into a smile for no reason. At this point, how could even the Seven Buddhas claim superiority?
Even Mañjuśrī’s face turned red and he stood bewildered. Today, the matter at Dongming is laughable; it causes people throughout the ages to waste their spittle.

"Fortunately, Master Hai has forgotten both self and non-self; the single thread of our school continues on and on. He then threw down his staff and said, "The burden of a thousand catties is now fully entrusted.
It was originally intended that this very staff would speak now. He struck three times with his whisk and descended from the seat.
The Master then entered the abbot’s quarters to pay his respects. On the following day, he said, "The old monk will not remain past this month. Upon reaching [the departure date],...

The Master still wished to withdraw and return to Dongting, but the fourfold assembly earnestly entreated him to remain, whereupon he succeeded to the seat [of the abbot]. He once raised the case of Xinghua asking the rector Kebin:
"Before long, you will become a master who leads the assembly. Kebin replied, "I do not enter this community. Xinghua said, "Do you enter it because you have understood, or because you have not?"
He did not enter. The guest said, "It is not like that at all. Huahua then struck him and said, "Venerable Kebin, you have lost the battle of dharma;
you shall be fined five strings of cash to provide a meal for the assembly in the hall. On the following day at the time of the midday meal, Huahua himself struck the wooden gavel and said:
Regarding the Vinaya rule for subduing a guest-monk: if one does not prevail in the "battle," one is not permitted to eat and must immediately be driven out of the monastery.
The Master took up the subject, saying: "If you are a descendant of the Ji lineage, you must certainly understand the affairs within his house.
In the past, I received a verse from the Elder Wanfeng and considered myself to have attained it; yet only today do I realize that I was wrong, while Wanfeng was not. (1)

Upon meeting Master Dongming, one realizes that [the function of] the staff consists of both reward and punishment. (While the punishment of the staff is easy to understand, the reward of the staff is difficult to recognize.

Only when one recognizes the reward of the staff can one truly hit the mark. The same applies to words and phrases. Indeed, while awakening resides within oneself, the Dharma relies upon the teacher. How could it be said that awakening once constitutes final completion?
To claim that awakening alone provides spiritual penetration and thus to seek neither teacher nor Dharma is precisely what is meant by "being without a teacher prior to the time of Vipaśyin."
This is acceptable. From the time after Vīrasvara onwards, this is how masters have transmitted it to one another. Thus, Kebin was able to recognize his father-teacher’s bitter heart;
he roused his own innate clarity and grasped the pivotal mechanism of the higher realm. He thoroughly penetrated the matters within the inner chamber; these cannot be fully expressed in words.
Even if his bones were crushed to dust, it would be difficult to repay even a fraction of Xinghua’s kindness—how much more so when he was beaten and expelled from the monastery?
This is precisely why the Elder Hai does not succeed Wanfeng today, but rather succeeds Dongming.

An ancient proverb says: "Only when raising a daughter does one know the mother’s suffering; only when fathering a son does one recognize the father’s toil. Truly, these words are so! There is indeed a great matter within this;
how could it be treated with such casualness? If one were to extract nails or split wedges for others, one must sit upon the lion throne.

Sons of the Buddha, you who sit upon the seat as teachers of humans and devas, who pluck out the cataracts from the eyes of men and succeed to the position of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, must pass through each and every point.

Do not mistake mere intellectual awakening for realization; do not trample upon the fundamental principles and set them aside without further inquiry. How would this differ from the demons and heterodox paths?
