(The speech of the ancients was like gold refined a hundred times; their opening words were like an experienced magistrate adjudicating a case. That later generations exhaust all their effort yet cannot catch up to them is because the ancients' realization was direct and solid. The Master happened—

While the Teacher was staying in the region between Han and Chu during the summer, it happened to be the season of late autumn. He was sitting on a stretch of land by the northern bank of the Jinsha River when two young boys were attending him.

The Master replied, "Worthy one, that which is secret is not a discourse; that which is a discourse is not the meaning. The other then stepped back one pace, rested his staff across his shoulder, and stood on one leg, asking, "What is this meaning?

At that time, the two monks were both startled and amazed, unable to fathom what had occurred. They asked, "What kind of śramaṇa was he?"
"What is the meaning of this? After a long silence, the Master said, "Do you two recognize this person?
Both monks replied that they did not. The Master said, "This is an Arhat and a worthy sage.
What he has presented is the Vajra King Transformation Samādhi and the Samādhirāja Samādhi; he has come to test me. Furthermore, he too possesses new realizations."

Songmen. Even up to the present day, there is nowhere to seek it. To the assembly: Those who have truly attained the Way possess minds that are ever leisurely and expansive;
they are solitary and non-active, straightforward and without artifice. They are like a cliff or a wall, solid and stable; they are like the great void of space.
It is without limit or obstruction; it is difficult to delineate or grasp. It has no flavor to be tasted; there is no method by which it can be sought.

Throughout the twelve periods of the day, one acts in accordance with conditions; every skillful means employed is clearly and distinctly understood. Like a newborn infant, the six faculties are at ease and free from substantial discrimination.
There is a metaphor in the teachings: [it is like] rolling a single [ball] upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
To take a single grain of mustard seed and cast it onto the tip of a needle at the foot of a mountain is truly an extreme difficulty. The Buddha said that even this is easy;
far more difficult than this is to attain birth in the human realm among the six paths of existence.

Now, having already obtained a complete set of physical features within this most difficult of circumstances, you clearly know that the Noble Path exists within your own body, yet you do not investigate and realize it for yourself.
They will readily cast themselves aside, whether they be foolish or wise; let the benevolent examine this carefully. The Master said to the assembly of gentlemen:

"I have often laughed at those Confucian scholars of old who slandered and rejected the Buddha, for it seems they had not investigated what the Buddha is, yet they felt constrained to denigrate and repudiate him.
What they call 'Buddha,' this is called 'Awakening' (*bodhi*). This so-called Buddha is one who, riding the wheel of great vows, manifested his traces among human beings."

He alone remains awake throughout the long night of the three realms; thus he is called the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One. This is truly an alternative designation for the Great Sage who has realized the truth and attained the Way.
He renounced affection and craving and abandoned honor and wealth, taking compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity as his mind.
He neither hoarded nor took; he was able to give and to save. "Not hoarding" refers not only to gold, jade, and the like, but truly to the afflictions of emptiness, delusion, and greed.

It is the residual habituation of this [practice], which is the complete, true, pure, and untainted merit. As for what is called "able to bestow," it does not merely refer to wealth, grain, and the like;
it directly reveals the unsurpassed, correct, and true Way, awakening sentient beings so that everyone may attain their own original mind and become a Buddha.
To speak in terms of the immediate, a Buddha is precisely the great essence and great function inherently possessed by every person.

It is simply the perfectly integrated true mind. Yet, people are naturally inverted; they turn their backs on true awakening and unite with delusive objects, thereby becoming confused and losing confidence in themselves.
Since they do not have confidence in the perfectly integrated true mind inherently possessed within themselves, they find no way to experience its fruition.
Consequently, they view other great sages as alien and harbor doubts toward them. When these doubts are not resolved, then—
Furthermore, they grow weary of and loathe it. As their loathing and detestation do not cease, they proceed to slander and reject it, claiming to possess great talent.
They believe that the Buddha has already been overturned by their refutations and that their own minds have attained sufficient satisfaction.
Moreover, regarding language and its meaning as the mere mechanism for weighing one particular region, where could they possibly recognize the Buddha? Thus they slander and reject the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "Furthermore, how can one know that one's own mind destroys its own mind, or that one's own mind opens up for itself?

It is like a calf butting its shadow; it does not know what the shadow is, nor from where it arises. Yet, intending to butt it, one person transmits a falsehood and ten thousand people transmit it as a reality;
one person acts it out and many follow suit, until those who imitate one another do so endlessly. Is this not so?"
To realize that these are but deluded acts is to see that they merely exhaust one's spirit in vain. Furthermore, it does not stop at merely exhausting the spirit;
one fears that at some future time there may be unforeseen calamities as their lingering consequences. Alas! Would not benevolent men and gentlemen feel a chill in their hearts upon hearing this?

He rose. Again he asked, "The Perfected Man has no dreams; why is this? The Master said, "Ordinary people, regarding the illusory and discriminating objects before them, do not know that their entire being is a dream.

This is what is meant by 'waking and sleeping are both dreams,' and dreaming within a dream."
The person of ultimate attainment knows the realm of their own mind as it truly is;

thus, regarding the illusory realms appearing before them, their wondrous functioning is serene and clear, penetrating all without obstruction, and even within sleep and dreams, they know them with clarity and remain awake with lucid discernment.

The thirty-fourth generation descendant of the Sixth Patriarch, Zen Master Miphan (Miyun) of Tiantong, whose name was Yuanwu, was the son of the Jiang family of Yixing, Changzhou. At the age of eight, he knew how to recite [the scriptures].

At thirty, he settled his wife and children and followed the transmission of the Yumen (Hugong) school. During the springtime, while wandering for recreation, he was constantly moved by the thought of the impermanence of the world. At fifteen, he was able to personally farm to support his parents.
At twenty-six, having read the *Platform Sutra*, he recited and studied it with joy, realizing there was a matter that transcended the mundane.

While carrying firewood into the market, he would set down his shoulder and stand across the main road, remaining unaware of the presence of others throughout the entire day. At thirty, he established his household and relied upon the lineage of Yumen.

He was still a layman, working as a cook and a hired laborer, carrying rice for a hundred *li*. At times he would speak of his own affairs; Chuan stared at him with fixed eyes, intermingling his inquiries with insults.
[Zhao’an] became despondent and fell ill. After twenty-one days, he recovered through purgation. He served in labor for four years before finally donning the monastic robes.
He shut himself within his room for a thousand days, vowing to clarify this matter. Chuan repeatedly subjected him to testing and examination, yet in the end [he could not find fault].
He granted permission. The Master himself also examined this, as if there were something—vivid and numinous—that he had ultimately failed to let go of.

"When hungry, eat; when thirsty, drink; sit at ease; sleep when weary. Within these four lines, there is one line that can both grant and take away, and can both kill and bring to life.

He replied, "The *Commentary on the Blue Dragon* (*Qinglong shuchao*). She asked, "Which sutra do you lecture upon? He replied, "The *Diamond Sutra* (*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*).
She said, "I have a question. If you can answer it, I will give you this snack; if you cannot answer it, you must go elsewhere. She continued, "The *Diamond Sutra* says: 'The past mind...'"
It cannot be apprehended. The present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. I do not know which mind the Elder was pointing to.
At that time, Deshan had no words. The Master said: "If I were Deshan, I would simply say, 'I am hungry, so pick out the largest ones and bring them here quickly!
This would have left the messenger and the old woman utterly at a loss, their hands flailing and feet stumbling as they struck out in confusion.
He did not set out immediately. When it came time to carry it away, he simply walked along with it on his shoulder. The nun in charge suspected that he had killed a traveling monk;

she thought he must have some extraordinary ability (Huilian said: "There is no extraordinary ability at all"). Yuanju asked Xianan, "What is the meaning of 'there is no extraordinary ability at all'? Xianan then went out. Yuan said:

He did not even need to ask once; [Wumen] hid his shadow and fled. He next asked Meian. Meian said, "Five times five is twenty-five. Yuan said, "You have not even dreamed of the stinking sweat of a patch-robed monk. He next asked Juefei. Juefei stepped forward, seized him, and said, "Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Yuan gave him a slap across the face.

Juefei pushed him away and said, "You little devil, why do you strike so recklessly? Yuan shouted, "Blind fellow! I am teaching you that the wicked person acts first. Meian said, "If one does not cut it off when it ought to be cut off, one will instead be outmaneuvered by the other.

Juefei gave him a slap and said, "Where was the point of failure? Here is where the root is pulled up. Meian laughed heartily. Ascending the hall, he stood before the seat and said, "The old monk’s breath..."
He gasped for breath and was unable to speak. He then coughed up phlegm onto the ground and said, "Brothers, try to say something.
After a long while, no one came forward. The Master wiped it away with his foot and returned to his quarters. Upon ascending the hall, he said, "If we discuss this matter..."
It cannot be described; it cannot be painted. Having swallowed Mount Cakravāḍa, he walks backward.
One phrase encompasses the sky and eighty thousand gates; every sentence is naturally free of leakage.

Zhaozhou’s barrier, Yunmen’s universality, Xuefeng’s rolling ball, Heshan’s beating the drum—this entire assembly of ancient worthies, when looked upon, are seen not yet to have mastered the lion’s roar. You!
"Everyone, you must shake off the path of turning back. If you can practice this, do not be attached to anything wherever you go, nor follow after others.
When pressed, turn yourself around and bite them; only then can you open your mouth wide before people.
But tell me, what does one use here at Yumen? Suddenly he brandishes his staff and says: 'A single staff, black as lacquer—saint or ordinary person, it splits them apart.'"
[The Master] leaned forward on his spine, gave a shout, and descended from the seat. Entering the hall, he cited the verse of National Teacher Shao: "At the summit of Tongyuan Peak...
The Master said, "Everyone is right here; it is not the human realm. [The Master] said, "A mistaken commentary. "There is no dharma outside the mind."
The Master said, "It suffocates people to death. Green mountains fill the eyes. The Master said, "Having eyes, yet being as if blind.
"Does the assembly still recognize National Teacher Shao? If you do recognize him, then the National Teacher Shao of the past and this old monk of today are not a failure of speech."

"Do not call it a whisk, and you will have finished with it. If you do not call it a whisk, you have finished. But what else would you call it?"
"What business is there to do? He strikes the incense table with his whisk and says, "The alert are alert; those who nod off are nodding off.
Yet, even if one calls them 'alert' or 'nodding off,' they still have no fundamental basis to rely upon. He lets out a shout and says, "I, this old monk, act according to the fundamental basis!
Thereupon, he descends from the seat. Ascending the hall for the discourse: "Today is precisely the seventh day of the first month; it is thus handed down in the world."
This is the day. How pitiable are those who have not yet awakened from their great dream; instead, they perceive shifts in weather and give rise to anger and speech.
This makes one recall the old Yunmen, who could say, "Every day is a good day. Brothers, do you know where Old Man Yunmen lands? After a long silence, he said:
"He is simply a black lacquer bucket that cannot distinguish black from white. He then added: "Every day is good."

"Is it not that you snatch it away and twist it out of shape, casting it elsewhere to burn? Do you call this 'meeting'? Yet, fundamentally, it is not this principle. Since it is not this principle, even these two characters 'meeting' (xiāngjiàn) are already superfluous.
What is the Dharma-gate of entering directly with a single blade? Heh! After thirty years, do not slander Xinyuan. Ascending the hall, he said:

"The first move at the head cuts off the vital ford. As soon as one tilts the ear, the family treasure is lost. From the beginning, the Buddha-dharma does not conform to human sentiment. Therefore it is said:"

"At the summit of Tongyuan Peak, what a wonderful message! If anyone can recognize it, their study of the Way is complete. He gave a shout and said, "No need to stand for long," and then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall again, he said: "The tenth day of the second month—what a wonderful message! All the people throughout the great earth [leap forth]."

Unable to leap out. He took a sip of tea and said: "In a hundred years, thirty-six thousand rounds; turning over and over, it is originally this thief. Ascending the hall, he raised the following case:

"The old man Yunmen speaking thus only answered the question regarding the Dharma-body; he did not yet [answer the phrase that penetrates it]."
Answer: To have penetrated the phrase of the Dharma-body. Suppose someone were to ask Jingshan today, "What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharma-body?
I would tell him: "Holding a night market within the eyes of a gnat; playing on a swing upon the tongue of a tiger. Tongyuan, however, does not do so.

[The assembly] understood. "Even if you do not understand, the words of Tongyuan remain. Ascending the hall for the opening of the furnace, [the Master said]:
"Prajñā is like a great mass of fire; if you attempt to approach it, it will burn away your face. He suddenly took up his staff and struck it repeatedly, saying:

"Those who do not shrink from the fire when at the furnace shall meet with this staff. [Lian said: "With heads scorched and faces burned, what can they do? Xixi said: "If one fears the blade and avoids the sword, what can they do?"]

"The flames preach the Dharma for the Buddhas of the three periods of time. How many strands of eyebrows must one watch over? The Buddhas of the three periods stand upon the ground and listen—distinctly so."

"Unlocated True Person. The Master said, "Right now, you are this very thing; you are the Unlocated True Person. (Another version says: "Head Master, do not let yourself be deceived!

"In practicing Chan, one must strictly avoid allowing various poisons to enter the mind; what is valued is purity and singleness. Therefore it is said: 'If you bring up one, you must not bring up two. To let slip one point is to fall into the second.
You must know that practicing Chan is the second, and cultivating the Yuanmen (Gate of the Origin) is also the second."
Becoming an immortal is secondary; becoming a Buddha is secondary; birth is secondary; death is secondary.
In short, whenever a single thought arises, it is all secondary. If you truly wish to understand, be pure and without admixture;
simply look back toward the moment before a single thought has arisen. Look while walking, look while standing, look while sitting, and look while lying down.
Look! Look! Looking, one does not know walking when walking; one does not know standing when standing; one does not know sitting when sitting;
one does not know reclining when reclining. Unaware and unknowing, suddenly there is a face-to-face encounter; only then does one realize that all along one has been applying the mind in error.
This was shown to Layman Shigong Lin. When the Patriarch came from the West, he did not establish written words; he pointed directly at the human heart alone. Only the ultimate virtue—
Mount Linji’s use of the staff and shouts to point directly is the most clear and essential method. As it is said: "The staff strikes the head of the stone man;
*pop*—he discusses the reality of things. Yet people today do not realize where the staff points, but instead take the sensation of pain and itching to be the mind.
Little do they know that this is merely the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*). An ancient said: "Those who study the Way do not recognize the True."
This is simply because people have recognized the spirit from the past. Throughout immeasurable kalpas, it has been the root of birth and death, yet deluded people mistake it for their original self.
Therefore, I asked the Layman: "What is it like when there is neither pain nor itch?
If you, Layman, wish to resolve the matter of birth and death and penetrate the nature of the spirit, simply look at this fan: where does it land?
Thus, one who naturally knows the Way is like a single blow; from the very beginning, it has never struck upon the site of pain.
It is truly as if a staff strikes the head of a stone man—one immediately perceives what the Great Master Linji said: "I was struck sixty blows by my late teacher Huangbo."
It is like being brushed by a stalk of mugwort; how could one who merely knows the sensation of pain and itching truly understand it?
To the practitioner Lin, I show that the Patriarch’s coming from the West was solely to point directly and hold up the essence, causing people to return to the root and revert to the source.
If you wish to investigate its meaning, simply look straight through, right before the state of neither seeing nor hearing, and you will see clearly at once. It is like this:
A black lacquer bucket exists within the darkness; from the beginning, there are not two colors, and thus there are no two views.
Since there are no two views, one does not see a male, nor does one see a female; one does not see bondage or liberation; one does not see ordinary beings or sages, nor purity or defilement.
Furthermore, one does not see the primordial or the wondrous, nor awakening or non-awakening; nor does one see a path.
I do not speak of it. I see neither emptiness nor non-emptiness; I see neither truth nor untruth.

Nor do I see suffering or pleasure, delusion or wisdom, the burning house or cool serenity. Therefore, throughout my life, whenever anyone comes to me, I simply strike them once with my staff, causing their wooden cask to shine with light so that they are free from dualistic views.
This is what is called "directly cutting through to the root," as certified by the Buddhas.
I address the Chan practitioner Jingxu: if you truly wish to transcend birth and escape death, you must cultivate an iron-and-stone heart, like withered wood or extinguished embers.
Let both sacred thoughts and mundane emotions be free from arising and ceasing. Upon this state of pure nakedness and brilliant clarity, you must realize and witness it through deep penetration;
seeing it through to the bottom and attaining firm conviction, you will walk hand-in-hand with the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity.

There must be no deviation. You must further practice such that ten thousand years are contained within a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment contains ten thousand years—pure and singular, without admixture.
Should even the slightest trace of arising or ceasing occur, it becomes the causal condition for birth and death, and there will be no time for liberation.
Strive to be like a bird escaping from a cage—without desire and without dependence. In every movement and action, always practice and walk the path within your own fundamental nature. Do not...

one takes "not resting until awakening" as one's path; and one takes "not resting until awakening" as one's vow. Once awakened, one then rides upon the power of that awakening to benefit oneself.
To benefit others through this, the diligent effort, the path, and the making of vows are all contained therein; there is no need for separate vows, a separate path, or separate effort.
Furthermore, once one truly awakens, every detail will be self-evident without needing to ask others.
Furthermore, I record that Layman Chang Chen said: "When studying the Way, one must first expect awakening; when the power of awakening is fully developed, it reaches the very crown of the head."

Following names and forms, one gives rise to successive distinctions of emotional consciousness; thus, according to the old state, there is no portion of self-sovereignty.

One should know that the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa is the great ocean, and discriminative wisdom is its raindrops. Although the drops differ from one another, they all ultimately return to the great ocean.
It is inherently without differentiation; that is to say, this alone is the one true reality, while the other two are not real.
This is the orthodox teaching and the correct purport. If there were a wisdom of differentiation that excelled nirvāṇa, that would be the teaching of Māra.

Chan Master Mingyu of Xiansheng Temple in Shaoxing Prefecture was the son of the Ding family of Qiantang. He possessed extraordinary qualities from birth.

At the age of eight, while playing with other children, he would chant Buddhist hymns (*brahman*). At fourteen, he abstained from meat and took delight in practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

A Chan practitioner rebuked him for this, instructing him to contemplate the "Patriarch of High Peak" koan. One day, upon being struck by the words of Master Pang, he composed a verse: [Verse omitted as per instructions]

At the age of twenty-three, he went to Zhenzong Yin to receive the tonsure. He delighted in extensive learning, but Yin would often suppress him. One night, while walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), he recalled the story of the old woman turning the Tripitaka.
Upon touching the incense table, he attained realization. When he presented this to Yin, Yin asked, "Have you awakened to the Way?"
The Master said, "I have not yet awakened to the Way, but I have caught Venerable Zhaozhou red-handed. Yinzhu asked, "Where did you see Zhaozhou? The Master then recounted what he had attained.
Yinzhu said, "What is that 'half-treasury'? The Master replied, "This is the matter of penetrating the Dharma-body. Yinzhu suddenly struck him across the face with his palm, and the Master withdrew.
Subsequently, he went to study under Yunmen. Upon entering the hall, he took a vow of silence; while he was intensely focused on his practice, suddenly—
Entering the hall, Nanquan shouted loudly, "Put it down! Master [Linji] could not help but lift his eyebrows and smile.
Nanquan asked, "When the ox in Huaizhou eats the grain, why does the horse in Yizhou have a bloated belly? The Master said, "Ask the pillar.
Nanquan said, "As for the tree falling and the vines withering, where ultimately does the phrase return? The Master said, "The long river turns its white waves. Nanquan said, "..."
"What is the phrase that cannot be exhausted by a single utterance? The Master said, "The crescent moon falls upon the solitary peak.
Wumen said, "I still have my doubts about you. The Master then composed a verse: Before Stone Umbrella Peak, a jade stream flows; Having reached the source, why speak of the boat lost in confusion?
Boundless fallen flowers as the spring mountains darken; Finding the path home, listen to the birds' cries. Wumen ridiculed him.
The Master shook his sleeves and departed. One day, while entering the inner chamber, [Zhimen] asked, "The dog has no Buddha-nature;
what do you think of this? The Master responded with a verse: "No Buddha-nature, no Buddha-nature. A scale-weight falls into the well, yet it floats.
Having once defeated Zhaozhou, I clap my hands all day long, singing the *zhègū*. Zhimen approved of this and subsequently entrusted him with the lineage. In winter, he followed [the Master].
Tiantong Wuyuanju stepped through the gate and gave a shout. Tiantong remained silent. The Master said, "To hesitate and let the mechanism of thought stop is the livelihood of ghosts.
He immediately left. A monk standing nearby said, "He has missed it. The Master struck him with his palm and said, "Raising troops after the battle is already over.

Upon hearing the news of Yunmen’s passing, he returned to wail at the portrait hall. When the assembly requested a small *śāstra* (small sermon), he cited the karmic conditions of Shishuang’s "The entire world has never been hidden."
[He] finished, saying: "O Great Assembly! It has not been hidden. The eastern wind sways the willow threads long; the red is full, the green is thin.
Fluttering butterflies cross the precarious wall; pairs of swallows circle the painted beams. Making the gesture of plucking the lute, he said: "In vain one wipes the silver lamp;
deep in the night, alone one regulates the *gong* and *shang* notes. He then gave a shout and descended from the seat. [On another occasion,] he ascended the hall and said: "The seamless."
The pagoda canopy covers the imperial palace; eating oil-cakes does not deceive the local deity. The Buddhas of the three periods possess wisdom yet remain in lowly positions;
the white oxen and stray cats lack virtue yet occupy high stations. It is not that the base is truly base, nor that the noble is truly noble.
"In total, they are not as good as the lamp-post and the lantern, which are skilled at harmonizing and uniting. Holding up his staff, he said: "This is the Samādhi of Non-contention.
He ascended the hall and said: "Having lit a lamp that requires no oil, I have opened wide the aperture at the crown of my head and entered the midst of the bustling marketplace."
Meeting the source at every turn, one attains the wondrous. How is it that Hanshanzi forgot the path he came by?

Ruan Ji was unrestrained; Sun Deng let out a long whistle. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Venerable assembly, after the World-Honored One held up the flower, has anyone yet brought forth this matter?
After a long silence, he said: "If you wish to know the price of rice next year, ask Wang the Great of the eastern village. Ascending the hall, [he spoke again].

It is best to rest, to rest; yet one does not rest. With white hair, one has passed the civil service examinations, yet still clings to the black fur robe. One vainly boasts of the yellow chrysanthemums' color after the frost;

white clouds and red trees fill the desolate mounds. Śāriputra, there is no reason for this. The sword has gone, yet you labor in vain to carve marks upon the boat. Truly, he is a scion of the Golden Wheel lineage;
how could he be content with the rank of a Marquis of Ten Thousand Households? Question: How does one penetrate through?

The monk said, "A censer has two handles. The Master said, "Not yet. Speak further.

Kung-fu. A monk asked, "How should I investigate the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Why have you gone down to the kitchen to steal turnips to eat?

Chan Master Mingfang Shiyu of Baoshou in Hangzhou Prefecture, whose courtesy name was Duànfuli, was born in Wutang, Jiaxing, as a member of the Chen family.
The son of this family possessed innate wisdom through his karmic cultivation; the sacred roots had been planted in him from an early age.

If there were such a person, then these two Mañjuśrīs would not perceive body, mind, or the world as separate, but would have forged them into a single piece.

He then descended to West Peak and again visited Yunmen. One day, as Yunmen ascended the hall, he said: "Let it go."
Upon hearing this, the Master attained sudden enlightenment; his entire being was filled with joy and liberation. He presented a verse, saying: "A single throw into the empty sky—no hesitation.

In the blink of an eye, wind and waves pervade the Great Void. Having realized the meaning of extending and retracting upon the tip of the pole, I see that the fish released were originally those caught on the hook."

Those in the world who speak of the Way do not have a single teaching. You ask me about the Way—is it not for the purpose of ending birth and escaping death, and seeing one's nature to become a Buddha?"
This Way cannot be attained through having a mind, nor can it be sought through being without a mind.
Li Lou has no means to employ his clarity; Shi Kuang has no means to employ his hearing; Gongshu Zi has no means to employ his ingenuity;
and Ning Wuzi has no means to employ his "foolishness. If one cannot forget the self, one cannot learn the Way; if one cannot forget the mind...
One cannot study the Way if one cannot forget the world. One cannot study the Way if one cannot forget fame.
One cannot study the Way if one cannot forget profit. One cannot study the Way if one does not forget wife, children, and kinsmen.
One cannot study the Way if one does not forget home, garden, and worldly affairs. One cannot [study the Way] if one does not forget knowledge and views.
To study the Way, one must record what is practiced and not forget it; one cannot study the Way if one is fond of relying on others;
one cannot study the Way if one craves ease and fears difficulty. Yet can the scholar-officials truly act in this manner? Nevertheless, who was Shun, and who am I?
Moreover, the Buddha is called the Honored One Among the Two-Legged Beings; how much less so are the scholar-officials, who possess no such merit.

Is there anyone who possesses such wisdom? If you do not squander this wisdom elsewhere, but instead resolutely see through the illusory nature of this body—realizing that with a single breath not continuing, it will immediately fall into decay—then since even this body is beyond grasping, what else outside the body could one possibly cling to?
Strive toward that time before heaven and earth were formed, and before human beings had yet arisen, [to find] yourself...
When body and mind are both non-existent prior [to this realization], one realizes for the first time the vast and expansive nature of one's own essence.
Only then does one know that self-nature is fundamentally pure, fundamentally complete, and fundamentally beyond arising or ceasing.

From the Son of Heaven down to the common people, there is not one who is unsuited to practice it, nor one who cannot reach its goal. How could it be said that scholars and officials are incapable of studying the Way?
A guest asked, "What kind of scholar-official finds it easy to study the Way? He replied, "One who is complete in three matters finds it easy to study the Way.

"What are these three matters? "First, knowing that there are the three periods of time. If one does not know that there are the past, present, and future, then those of superior capacity may strive to become sages and worthies, yet they will not reach heights of loftiness;
as for those of inferior capacity, even their ordinary cultivation and self-examination will likely not suffice—how much less so [the Way]!"

One may discuss with such a person the Way that transcends the world. Second, one who knows the terrors of the three periods of time but, knowing them, does not fear them, differs from one who is ignorant by only a small margin.
Third, one who understands the three periods of time but, though fearing them, does not fully comprehend them, will ultimately be ensnared by the three periods.
As for what is meant by "knowing," it refers to clearly seeing the fallacy of the theory of the extinction of nature; yet those who see with their eyes and hear with their ears commit many errors.
The resonance between present and future must not be doubted. The favorable or adverse conditions encountered in this life stem from the good or evil deeds committed in previous lives;
the good or evil deeds performed in this life determine the favorable or adverse conditions one will encounter in future lives.

First, one should remain content with one’s lot and accept circumstances with equanimity; second, one should guard against the slightest transgression and prevent small faults from escalating. Why is it said that one should "remain content with one’s lot"?

To receive [the fruits of karma] is as follows: to be born virtuous yet meet an early death, or to be upright yet suffer hardship, all depend upon causes from previous lives; there is nothing for which one may harbor resentment.

To be born wealthy yet remain greedy, or to live long yet remain callous, all evoke results for future lives; there is no room for侥幸 (reckless hope). One who understands this possesses the disposition for studying the Way.
As for what is called "fear," it is the intense mindfulness that the cycle of saṃsāra continues uninterrupted throughout the three periods of time.
A single moment’s lapse can cause one to suddenly ascend or sink to vastly different states. Not only is evil to be feared, but even goodness is not something to be relied upon.
Even if one’s cultivation in this life is perfect, who knows that in a future life one will not become deluded while dwelling in favorable circumstances?
It has never happened that one who understands this yet remains unconcerned, sleeping and sitting at ease or eating and drinking with no sense of urgency. Such is the nature of true fear.

There exists a graduated path for training on the Way. That which is called "clarity" refers to the fact that the delusions of the three periods of time are fundamentally rooted in a single confusion.

Because in previous lives one was confused regarding one's own true nature, one identified external objects as the self, took the four great elements to be the body, and took that which arises in response to objects to be the mind.
Thus, one increased deluded thoughts and deluded karma, thereby bringing about this present life of a deluded body and a deluded world. Now, in this present life, one is again confused.

Regarding one's own original nature: to mistake external objects for oneself and fail to realize that the four elements are illusory and that the mind is fundamentally unborn, leads to the proliferation of deluded thoughts and deluded karma in the present, thereby creating a deluded body and a deluded world in future lives.
If one aspires to the dharma-gate of the swift path—the one sought by the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity through countless kalpas of enduring every hardship and suffering—it teaches people:
Before the body, mind, and world had yet come into being, consciousness was already its own original nature; thus it was fundamentally unborn from the beginning—how could there be anything to cease?
Even in the present, it cannot be apprehended; how then could there be a past or a future? Only then does one know that there is no person and no thing:
the ten directions and the world-ocean are but bubbles, and all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning brushed away. Thereafter...
It is not an obstacle to mount the wheel of one’s own vows and manifest birth and death within the realm where there is no birth and death;

to manifest body and world within the realm where there is no body or world; and to manifest the three periods of time within the realm where there are no three periods of time. Appearing and disappearing, contracting and expanding, all are like dreams and illusions.
Only those who seek such realization can truly study the Way. The Official asked: "How should one study the Way so as not to stray from the path?"
He said, "Excellent is this question! Among those in the world who do not participate in the Chan of the Nirvana Hall, it is difficult for them not to go astray.

Nevertheless, those who transmit the Dharma today fill the world; they practice universal compassion, making no distinction between the pure and the defiled, proclaiming the teachings without restriction, and delivering all who harbor doubts or slander.
Those who have advanced before take broad accessibility as their heart's aim, while those who follow behind find it easy."
I entered [the discussion] for this purpose: to recognize that while names flourish, the substance declines; and to discern that what appears similar in name is actually not so in reality.

How could it be said that such discourse is entirely non-existent? I dare say it is rare. Yet, as for my own words, how could they be sufficient to be valued by others, such that I might venture to discuss them deeply with you?
The guest pressed his request, saying: "If you do not reject words simply because of the person who speaks them, I shall briefly engage in some idle conversation with you."
Those who study the Way should not harbor the sighs of those who failed to reach their goals, such as those of Wu Shou, Yue, or Yan. First, one must resolve with sincerity and correctness.

If one’s aspirations are small and one’s vision limited, seeking only to become a virtuous person of the mundane world, it will suffice to read the books of the sages and worthies of this world and practice the deeds of those sages and worthies.
Alternatively, if one follows the expedient teaching methods of the Tathāgata to assist in cultivation and self-examination, this too will be beneficial.
There is no harm. If you wish to ultimately realize the unsurpassed, wondrous Way that transcends the world, you must first single-mindedly focus on birth and death.

If you single-mindedly focus on birth and death, then even if your learning is vast and your memory as sharp as that of Ānanda, your ability to answer ten questions with one as seen in the case of Ghaṇṭā, your being honored by birds bringing flowers as in the case of Goshirshaka, or your having a thousand fingers circling your seat as in the case of Jiashan, you still must set aside your own views and follow others—how much more so for those who are inferior?
Those who fall below this level do not seek to transcend birth and death, yet they must value knowledge and views; this Way does not belong to knowledge and views.

They do not seek to transcend birth and death, yet they must strive for efficacy and power; this Way does not belong to efficacy and power. They do not seek to transcend birth and death, yet they must admire unrestrained license;
this Way does not belong to unrestrained license. To value knowledge and views, to strive for efficacy and power, or to admire unrestrained license—these are not the ways of the ignorant.

This leads immediately to madness; one becomes a demon and falls outside the Way. To bring forth evil fruits from good causes is mostly the result of those who study the Path for the sake of birth and death without focused diligence.
Is this not a single misstep that results in a perpetual straying? Second, one must apply oneself with diligent effort and correctness.

Having already resolved to study the Path for the sake of transcending birth and death, can one not turn back upon oneself to reflect and examine? If one truly possesses the great capacity, upon hearing [the teaching] once...
Even after a thousand awakenings, you may still not have realized it. If you have not yet attained it, you must investigate a single phrase of the *huatou*.

If you do not penetrate it in one day, you must investigate for one day; if you do not penetrate it in one month, you must investigate for one month; if you do not penetrate it in one year, you must investigate for one year;
if you do not penetrate it in one lifetime, you must investigate for the next life. Only when there is never any falling back and never any change can it be called [true realization].

The earnest practice of investigating a single phrase of the *huatou* is the sharp blade that cuts through the dense forest of intellectual views, the compassionate vessel for crossing the bitter sea of birth and death, the sacred medicine that dissolves the various poisons entering the mind, and the guiding teacher who points out the lost path of ten thousand ages.
Without accumulating merit, it accumulates of itself; without severing evil, it severs it of itself; without observing the precepts...
He is naturally disciplined; without practicing concentration, he is naturally concentrated; without cultivating wisdom, he is naturally wise; without exhorting the Buddha, he naturally exhorts him;
without reciting the sutras, he naturally recites them; without seeking birth in superior realms, he naturally attains birth in superior realms;
without seeking many virtuous friends, he naturally has many virtuous friends. Originally he sought no praise, nor was he subject to blame. Thus he is singularly focused; thus it is.
Exert diligence! Even if such illumination has not yet been achieved after such a long period, it can still serve as a model for later students.
In the future, you will surely attain the heart-essence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

If, however, you treat names and forms as the path to liberation from birth and death, giving rise to peripheral doubts and seeking external aids, conceiving heterodox views and wandering outwardly, fearing hardship while delighting in easy shortcuts, then hundreds of delusions will surely converge within you.
How could its errors be fully described? Third, one must awaken to the point with absolute certainty.

Since you are single-mindedly and exclusively investigating birth and death, you must wait until your skill is perfected and your effort exhausted; only when the time comes will the principle manifest, the life-root be severed, and the original face appear.
Do not harbor doubts regarding birth and death; do not harbor doubts regarding antiquity and the present; do not fall into pits or trenches; do not forcibly assume the role of a sovereign;
do not identify with the conscious spirit; do not sink into a void; do not engage in hypocrisy or confusion; do not enter the deceptive circles of false teachers;
do not violate the discernment of those with clear vision. Otherwise, you will mistake fish eyes for pearls, mistake drowsiness for death, and take reckless assumption to be true power.
To take rigid distinctions as being beyond doubt; to take coarse, reckless, and chaotic behavior as the great function of the great capacity;

to take superficiality as thorough liberation—these are errors. One should advance further on the tip of the staff but does not advance; one should investigate the words and phrases but does not investigate;

one needlessly engages in forced analysis when there is no need for it; one attempts to brush away what cannot be brushed away. Having missed the entrance by a single step, various heterodox interpretations become entangled.

I say: that which is truly fit for bitter weeping, shedding tears until they flow, and long-drawn sighs—is it not this very thing? Fourth, one must ensure that the lineage of masters is authentic and correct.
It is not merely a matter of avoiding those teachers who lack a true transmission and fabricate their own doctrines; one must also be wary of those who merely echo what they have heard from others.

Even when following an unbroken stream of succession, one must examine the actual conduct and realization of the master; one must not blindly shoulder the burden of the lineage’s rope and falsely claim authority for oneself.
Have you missed the point where the Master acts for your sake? Have you not been struck by the deep thrust behind the head from the Master?
Have you thoroughly clarified the ancestral lineages and principles? Have you not acted with partiality, thereby blinding the eyes of men?

If there were no authentic master of the school to strike blind the eye at the crown of your head and snatch away the talisman from your elbow, then even if you possessed genuine realization, it would be of no avail.
If one understands for oneself, it is acceptable; but if one acts for others, calamity arises.

Should one’s own vision already be biased and what one imparts to others be further erroneous—while claiming for oneself a state of empty vastness, yet falling under the sway of blind blows and blind shouts—it is like water merging with water or space merging with space.
One falsely grasps the Vajra-treasure sword, believing that the total destruction of all things is reality, unaware that within the treasury of our King there is no such blade.
The blind lead the way for sentient beings; like rivers flowing ever downward, some enter a realm of triviality, becoming stained by the flavors of perverse knowledge and evil interpretations.
This poisonous perversity enters the heart like oil into flour, yet they remain unaware of their error, claiming instead that they have attained self-acceptance.
They refuse to receive ultimate instruction from others, asserting that they are not being led astray by anyone else. Or again, they say, "My own view is correct."
Bottom line: as long as one has practiced and realized it, why should such things even be worth mentioning? Fifth, one must be precise at the very end.
Only the final phrase reaches the secure barrier. For the numinous tortoise to carry the diagram is to bring upon itself the omen of its own death.
If one does not penetrate the final secure barrier, yet claims to have attained great capacity and great function—if one does not penetrate the final secure barrier, yet claims...
Those who possess the basic provisions of grass and fodder are rare, for few are not coarse and unruly vagabonds.
If one has not penetrated this barrier, even if they possess correct awakening, they may still be called a teacher who guides others at a particular time;

yet if they lack correct awakening and do not know that such a barrier exists, then regarding the ancient masters' practice of investigating and awakening, and their subsequent re-doubting after awakening—where the later does not displace the former—they merely point to awakening as if it were something fixed.
Those who do so are rare among the deluded. To slander the ancient sages and mislead future generations stems entirely from not knowing the ultimate barrier beyond;

How can one not be vigilant and earnest? Sixth, one must ensure that the Path Truth (mārgasatya) is authentic.

Seventh, one must be sincere and authentic toward others. One must not impart the true Dharma to people. One must not deceive people by saying, "I have expedient means to help you enter [the Way] easily.

Chan Master Mian of Tiantong inscribed the epitaph for his stupa. He authored the *Zongmen Chengfan* (Exemplary Models of the School Gate) in four volumes, which, along with his recorded sayings, have been circulated in the world.

Chan Master Wenda Ruan’an of Nanjian Lian’an in Hangzhou was the son of the Yu family of Wujiang. Having lost his mother at a young age, he fell seriously ill and developed a fondness for drinking wine.
At the age of sixteen, he was suddenly struck with alarm and said to himself, "How can I allow my body and mind to have no place to rest?
He resolved to apply himself to study. One day, while passing by a mountain temple, he saw the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and read these words: "This..."
Body and mind, extending outward to empty space, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all are things within the wondrously luminous true mind.
Having doubts, he went specifically to visit Xiu of Qingshan, who instructed him to contemplate the koan: "The original face before one's parents were born.
One day, while Xiu was standing by a mountain stream with a guest, holding up the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Master opened his mouth. Suddenly, Xiu asked: "How is it?"
This was his own mind; at that time, he did not realize he had lost it himself. At the age of twenty-four, pressured by the hardships of marriage, he fled in the dead of night.

Upon reaching Wulin, he left the household life (took the white robe). He once knelt before a Buddha lamp at night, single-mindedly holding the phrase "the original face before one's parents were born," but failing to attain realization, he resolved to travel to study under various masters.
Hearing that Master Wu of Jinsu was at Beichan, he packed his bag and set out.
He hurried to Wuzhong, where he received a severe beating as an instruction. He then went up to Qingshan, where he again met Master Shanzu Ji.

While staying together in the mountains, at the fifth watch of the night, he heard the sound of a gale; his doubts were instantly resolved. Before his eyes, all was bare and naked, with not a single dharma to obstruct the mind.
He felt a profound sense of joy throughout his entire being and composed a verse, which begins: "A thousand origins, ten thousand..."

if this view is not eliminated, how can one ever hope to transcend birth and death? Thus Yongjia said: "In practicing cultivation, I fear falling into the pit of annihilation and permanence.
Furthermore, there are those who insist on seeing this original person, day after day feeling for it in the void and grasping at shadows.
Shadow. Raising one's eyebrows and staring with bulging eyes—like a thirsty deer chasing a mirage until old age and death.
The person of original nature ultimately has no place for you to grasp. If you wish to cast off such views and such ailments, you must seek a decisive breakthrough beneath the great staff;
then the sickness of the Buddhas, the sickness of the Patriarchs, the sickness of Zen, the sickness of birth and death, and the sickness of the four hundred and four afflictions will all be resolved.
Regarding the eighty-four thousand afflictions and even the various evil views of non-Buddhist schools,
one finally attains peace of mind only when there is no longer any ground upon which they can take root.
