The thirty-sixth generation descendant of the Sixth Patriarch, Chan Master Wutai Goutui Buiting Xingyong of Nan Yue, was the son of the Han family in Qiantang, Hangzhou. From childhood he had been fond of the Buddha-dharma;
when he reached the age of twenty-one, he urgently desired to leave the mundane world, but his parents would not permit it. He subsequently fled by night and arrived at Jie.
At Sanseongsa, he paid his respects to the abbot, Master Yeonbibi, and accompanied him along with Jeonam Jin to visit the Elder Daegak at Bogeunsa.

There, he exerted himself in investigating the koan of "the state before one's parents were born. Later, while participating in a communal work request (*pujeong*), he saw a monk walking along carrying an empty basket on his shoulder.

He attained a realization. One day, while attending Master Jue, Jue asked a monk, "It is easy to turn the mountains, rivers, and the great earth back into oneself, but it is difficult to turn oneself back into the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
How do you understand this? At that moment, the Master [Zhaozhou] thoroughly penetrated the very source of the Dharma from the side.

At that time he was twenty-five years old. Thereafter, his side never touched the mat as he attended morning and evening consultations; day by day he reached the ultimate depths of the profound mysteries.
Daoyue said to his teacher, "Since attaining the [Bodhisattva] stages, I have rarely seen anyone who has neglected sleep and forgotten food like this. He repeatedly invited him to share his seat.
The Master declined the offer with great earnestness and retired to the Yunfu Hermitage on Mount Daxiong, where he thatched a hut of reeds. In the winter of the Bingxu year, Jue traveled north;

the Master remained at Baen Temple as its head administrator for three years, through both cold and heat. He was sincere and earnest in his character, and his responses to seekers were swift and incisive, earning him the deep admiration of those far and near.
In the spring of the Wuzi year, Jue sent from Mount Jing a *kāṣāya* robe and a dharma verse to the three men of Chongfeng Peak.
At the same time, he received a prophecy. In the spring, he returned to Jue-nan; during the summer retreat, he stayed at Daxiong; and by winter, he had passed through Baoen.

There, he was specially commissioned to ordain monks and preside over the whisk (bifú). In the spring of the Ji-chou year, as Jue retired to Chongfu at Daxiong, the Master accepted an invitation to reside at Fahai in Wuxing.
In the autumn of the Xin-mao year, he traveled to Mount Lu and ascended Mount Heng; disciples followed his reputation like wind, requesting him to open the Dharma there.
At Mount Tiantai, a monk asked, "What is the iron snake boring into the diamond eye? The Master said, "A dragon slumbers in the ink-well.
"What is the Kunlun riding an elephant with a heron leading the way? The Master said, "An oxhorn rhinoceros stands alone on the sea.
"What is the mud-ox at the bottom of the sea chewing the moon as it runs? The Master said, "The pillar conceives a child."
"What is this rock tiger by the cliffside, cradling its cubs as it sleeps? The Master said, "A pile of bones rises from level ground.
He then presented a verse: The dog carries a lamp in its mouth down the street; The rat steals salt and returns with a snort. The pillar before the hall startles the dream to break;
Opening the door in the snow, one releases a tortoise. "Within these four lines of mine," he said, "there is one line that possesses expedient means (*upāya*)."
"It has substance; it has illumination and function. It can grant and it can take away; it can kill and it can bring to life.
If you can discern and grasp this, I will allow you to buy straw sandals and travel as a wandering monk. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him out directly.
Two monks prostrated themselves. The Master said, "Both of you have been studying the True Man of No Rank. Try to speak! The two monks were speechless.
The Master said, "I had a dream yesterday. I dreamed that a person from Japan went to Jiangxi, a place where bowls are made, and commissioned a ceramic Guanyin.
He placed it in a lacquered gold bucket and loaded it onto his ship.
As he was about to land back in his own country, the mooring ropes suddenly snapped, capsizing the vessel entirely, including the Great Compassionate One."
The layman did not see him; he simply pushed over the table as the voice spoke. (Guanyin appeared. A monk asked, "What is the student's nostrils?
The Master said, "You have no nostrils. The monk pressed further, "Where do you usually breathe out?
The Master struck him with his palm and said, "I told you you had no nostrils; where else would you breathe? A layman requested instruction.
The Master said, "Who have you seen? The scholar said, "I have seen Master Daxiong. The Master said, "Where did you meet him? The scholar said, "We met in the refectory.
The Master took up his staff and struck him out directly. The Master called to a monk, saying, "I am not asking about your practice;
bring me a Buddha. (On behalf of the monk, he slapped him across the face and said: "Namo Dunzhifu (Homage to the Buddha Who Is Too Indolent)."

A monk invited the Master to come. The Master reached out his hand and said, "If you cannot say it, I will give it to you. As the monk was about to respond, the Master struck him across the face with a blow.
The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him again. A monk brought tea to the Master. The Master took it and immediately slapped him.

(Why did he not return the salutation with a punch? The monk asked, "Where does my fault lie? The Master held up two fingers. (One case has not yet been settled, and another arises. The monk hesitated, and the Master slapped him once more.

Whenever the Master saw a monk enter, he would seize him and ask, "How many eyes do you have? (Just as the monk was about to strike him in the face with his palm,) the monk hesitated, and the Master struck him out.
A monk asked, "Why did the Great Sage of Sizhou appear in Yangzhou? The Master struck him.
The monk stepped forward and said, "There is no place for the Master to lay his hand. (It would have been well to strike him and drive him out. The Master struck him again. The monk hesitated.

The Master struck him again. The monk bowed and said, "The night is deep and the watches have passed; I pray that you, Master, will show us respect. The Master drew a line with his staff and said, "Speak!
Speak! The monk wiped it away with his sleeve. (At the fifth watch drum, he was caught for wandering at night. The Master struck him repeatedly with his staff and drove him out.
He then asked, "What is your original face? The Master said, "I do not even know myself. As the monk hesitated, the Master [struck him].
"Hai! [The Master] asked a monk behind him. (He struck him with his palm and said, "For now, strike the one in front. The monk said, "Where can one look to see it?
The Master said, "A hairless lock rattles at both ends. The monk hesitated; the Master then pushed him out. A monk came to pay his respects.

The Master asked, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From the road below. The Master said, "On the road below, I did not see you, that monk. The monk replied, "Please, Master, keep your eyes open.
The Master said, "Why do you not prostrate? The monk then performed a prostration. (On behalf of the monk, one might say: "A prostration is not a refusal;

yet one must still explain the matter. The Master said, "You have lost my descendants. The Master asked the Chief Steward, "If you call it a 'bamboo stick,' it is an obstruction. If you do not call it..."
[The Master] was holding a bamboo whisk when he turned his back [toward the student]. "Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The Abbot shouted; the Master also shouted. The Abbot shouted again.
The Master drew a line with the bamboo whisk. The Abbot hesitated, and the Master struck him out with a continuous blow of the staff.
A student asked, "Before the birth of one's parents, what is the student’s original face? The Master said, "In a village of three households, there is an ox that has only one horn."

Small Sermon for the Closing of the Retreat. Question: "The furnace is now fully opened to smelt the ordinary into the sacred. Before leaving Tuṣita Heaven and before emerging from the mother’s womb, how may one communicate this?
The Master said: "The frost strikes the banana tree; it is bare and lustrous. The student asked further:
"Once he has left Tuṣita Heaven and emerged from the mother’s womb, what then? The Master said: "His head shall split into seven pieces. The Master then said: "Three..."

A dilapidated hut pierces through the celestial eye; a seven-foot black staff brushes against the vast void. To clarify the three fundamental principles of Linji, one dances the *zhazi* within a thicket of thorns.

Last night, the "True Person of No Station" rode backward upon a three-legged donkey straight up to the crest of a ten-thousand-fathom peak, wishing to deliver a message to all of you. Suddenly striking his staff, he descended from the seat.
Small Assembly. The Master said: "Before leaving Tuṣita Heaven, he had already descended into the royal palace; before emerging from his mother’s womb, his work of saving beings was already complete.
Is there anyone here who has had a sudden flash of realization? He then spoke a verse: "In the land of Silla, fire burns; In Wu and Yue, stone men have their feet scorched.
Master Zhì discards his staff and scissors, And knocks down Fenggan, who dwells at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai."
At the base of the wall, within the Prince’s Hall at Fenyang, a flat-beaked wild duck from Gaoyou suddenly sprang forth.
Upon meeting anyone, it would bow its head and say, "Master! Master! Then, looking left and right, it would ask, "Do you understand?
After a long pause, it said: "Since Yuansha departed, there has been no news; on every branch, red and white, no flowers bloom."—Small Lecture by the Master.
"It is mind, it is Buddha"—Mañjuśrī was caught by the thief. "It is not mind, it is not Buddha"—Samantabhadra cried out in distress.
"Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing"—Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva touched upon a great knot at the tip of a hair.
Suddenly bumping into the pot-bellied Maitreya at the crossroads, he dropped his sack and laughed heartily.
He laughed and said, "The blue sky and bright sun—why are they being robbed? **Small Assembly Sermon (入室小參):** The Master asked a monk, "Xuefeng rolls the ball;
Daowu dances with his ritual tablet; Tianlong points his finger; Luzu faces the wall.

Is there any distinction of superiority or inferiority among them? The monk said, "And what about you, Master? The Master made a cutting motion with his hand toward his mouth and made a gurgling sound. The assembly was at a loss.
The Master said: "A single note of the Qiang flute at evening on the parting pavilion; you head for Xiangxiang, I head for Qin. Furthermore, a monk asked:
"If both you and I are burned until we become two heaps of ash, where shall we meet? The Master said: "Your feet are worn through, yet your straw sandals remain.
In a small lecture (xiao can), the Master said: "Nanquan said: 'Last night at the third watch, I lost my ox; when I rose at dawn, it was gone.'"
"Quelling the Fire. This old fellow speaks with his mouth full, yet he only manages to say eighty percent of it. Last night, Head Seat Yong bought a black old woman for three copper coins;
her head was flat and her eyes were large. He wished to introduce her to you all, but fearing that you would laugh at him, he performed a woman’s bow and said:
"May the Great Assembly have ten thousand blessings! Upon entering the room for the small *chan* (meditation) discourse, the Master showed [the following]:
The verse says: Where there are no traces, one fixates on contemplation; Excessive fixation on contemplation leads to fierce self-doubt.
Suddenly, the skull is smashed to pieces, And from the crow’s nest flies forth a phoenix chick. It further says: Do not miss the opportunity where there are no traces;
A white-nosed Kunlun sits right in the middle of the road. Last night fire burned the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven; The four sages and six classes of beings have nowhere to hide.
He managed to pass through; half a skull was missing. In a casual tug, he pulled open three [seals].
An old woman sat facing him. Small Assembly: An oil jar hangs from a crow’s beak; The moon sets behind the cold pines, causing a startle.
A cry escapes the mouth and the beak falls along with it; Meeting people, it calls out two or three times. Tell me, what is it calling? Suddenly—!
[The Master] gave a shout and held a small *sǎn* (informal discourse). A monk asked, "The Buddha said there are 'no sentient beings to be saved.
Why, then, are there so many here? The Master raised his staff and said, "What do you see? The monk stepped forward and said, "Truly, there are no sentient beings to be saved."
"Why do you strike? The Master said, "I knew well that you would understand it as striking. He then said: "Frequently calling for Little Jade, there was originally no business;

one simply wishes for the husband to recognize the sound. Long ago, when the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, saying, "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.
This was the World-Honored One acting before the time of Wei-yin (Vipaśyin).
Bān picks up his precious blade and carves up the world into pieces, intending to cause people to return to their original source.
Alas, throughout this Sahā World, everyone mistakes the servant for the master and calls a bell a jar. Fortunately, there was the old man of Shao Yang who said:
"Had I seen him back then, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to a dog, so as to ensure peace throughout the world. The old man of Shao Yang—
Han: "The stone woman is forbidden from giving birth. Elder Yong, based on the facts, closed the case and conveyed the message, ordering everyone to have their fill and then stop.
The assembly stood waiting; the Master then spoke this verse: "The turtle in the jar transforms into a rooster."
The mute opens the door and flies away; crawling up, he falls down, yet manages to grasp it.
To whom can this obvious truth be told? The Master enters the hall and says: "The eyebrows and eyes are very close together; why do they not see each other?
Is it perhaps because they are obstructed by the nose? The assembly remains silent. The Master says: "Do not say there is no birth and death," and then he leaves the hall. He opens [the door].
Small Assembly at the Incense Burner. O Zen practitioners with copper heads and iron brows, you carry the life-taking talisman slung across your elbows.

Yet there remains this incense burner that you cannot swallow; refine and polish your ice-cold liver and gallbladder. Suddenly, turning your body from south to north, you sit amidst the flames within the land of China.
[The Master] throws down his staff, calls to the assembly, and says, "Look at the fire! He then descends from the seat. *Thanks to the Two Orders.*
Small Assembly (Xiaocan). Shao-lin’s wall-gazing: white jade carved into the bones of Xi Zi. The snow-courtyard elbow-drop:

yellow gold cast into the heart of Wu Yuan. Six ears do not share a secret; one flower opens into five petals. [The Master] lets out a sudden shout and calls out in a loud voice to the newly appointed members of the two orders.

He descends from his seat. Small Assembly. The Master says: "Sand is scattered before the eyes; it cannot be seen. "Rice is in the chest; it cannot be swallowed. [He] lets out a sudden shout. Descends from his seat.
The brambles prick the mouth so it cannot swallow; they reach the cheeks, so one cannot even contemplate them. A blow across the spine with the staff leaves no room for evasion. Ha!
Linji was not yet a "white-thief" (a master thief who takes without a trace). But tell me, what kind of eyes do I, this mountain monk, possess?
[He strikes the meditation staff. "A date was set, but he did not come; the night passed midnight. Idly tapping the chess pieces, the lamp-flower fell. Small Assembly Sermon. The Master said:
Raising his left fist, he said: "The person is taken away, but the environment is not. Raising his right fist, he said: "The environment is taken away, but the person is not.
Grasping his left wrist, he said: "Both person and environment are taken away. Grasping his right wrist, he said: "Neither person nor environment is taken away.
You all—your very lives and souls—have been swallowed up in one gulp by this fist. If you can turn yourself around here, vomit it out.

He has obtained the breath. The whale swallows the seawater until it is exhausted, and the coral branches are revealed. If you cannot turn your body and cannot spit out your breath, [the Master] plants his staff and says:
"Next year there will be new branches; the spring wind that disturbs them shall never cease.
In a small lecture (xiao can), he cites an ancient saying: "What is there within the mountains? On the ridges, many white clouds. They can only bring solace to oneself."
Yue said, "I cannot bear to present this as a gift to you. Master Qing Shan laughed heartily and said, "White clouds—whose private property are they?
He pointed his whisk toward the sky and said, "Look! Look! The Master said, "Those two great elders were merely writing on the clouds and painting in the air.
At Gao Tai, it is not so. What does one have within the mountains? Only two piles of firewood. Hand them over to the head cook and burn them all away."
[The Master] arranged it again. In it there was one phrase that was inappropriate. Someone pointed it out, and [the Master] handed over his staff.
(The "Shang Daren" [text] has been put away; you, "Xiaosheng," should know propriety. A monk came forward and said, "There is not even a single piece of firewood.
The Master said, "To be wide awake in a dream. Another monk said, "What is the use of making two piles? The Master said, "A hound chasing after clods of earth. Another monk said, [and so on].
"The mountain ends and the water runs out; what can be arranged? The Master said, "Frozen to death, starved to death. He then looked around him, left his seat, and descended.
In the spring of the Yiwu year of the Shunzhi era (1655), the Master grew weary of worldly distractions. Taking up his staff, he retired to a remote peak and shut himself within a single room.
He cut off all contact with attendants, emulating the intent behind Xifeng’s "death-meditation retreat. On the sixth day of the fifth month, the Master manifested signs of illness.
He cast [the bowl] away, then rose and sat in the full lotus posture. Wiping his face with both hands, he passed away in serene stillness.

The Master was born on the nineteenth day of the ninth month of the Ding-si year of the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty. He entered parinirvāṇa on the eighth day of the first month of the Yi-wei year of the twelfth year of the Shunzhi era of the Qing dynasty.
He was thirty-nine years of age and had held the monastic precepts for seventeen years. The following year, his disciples...
Chaozhen and others escorted the remains back and constructed a stupa at Zhongwan in Zuxi, Yushan, Jiangyin. Master Feng composed the inscription for it.
At Ba’en Temple in Wukang County, Huzhou, there was the Dharma Master Chunchan, whose conduct was pure; he was from Yanping Prefecture, Fujian.
He was a native of Lèxiàn. His secular surname was Xióng. He became an orphan at fourteen and married at eighteen, fathering a son.
At the age of twenty, his wife and son both passed away in succession. Fearing that his worldly life was transient and lacking permanence, he resolved to leave the household life.
He went to his maternal uncle, Master Xíng Rú, and received the tonsure. He first visited Chan Master Qiǎn Rán Mì of Shòuchāng, who immediately recognized him as one of great capacity.
One day, seeing an ancient worthy’s instruction that said, "When a single breath does not come again, where will you go? a state of doubt suddenly arose within him.
Unconsciously, he let out a loud cry of weeping, then raised his arms and proclaimed: "I shall have nothing to do with any right or wrong!"
He proceeded directly toward unsurpassed Bodhi. My teacher was unaware that Commandant Li had spoken these words.
After I, this wandering staff-bearer, succeeded to the seat at Shouchang, I finally received full ordination; from then on, my practice became even more diligent and progressive.

Throughout both winter and summer, I wore only a single robe and a single garment of ramie cloth. During the coldest months, I would bind straw around my belly for sustenance, never allowing such austerity to disturb my mind.
In the winter of the Guiwei year, I passed by Boshan and entered the meditation hall. I then made a vow, saying: "If I do not clarify the Great Matter, I shall not leave this hall.
I applied myself with such intense pressure that for over forty days it was as if a rat were trying to enter a cow's horn.
Suddenly, struck by the sound of the hall bell before me, my entire being leaped out as if from a net. I was then twenty-seven years old. Throughout...
He traveled through the monastic centers of Minzhong and Jiangyou, staying for only one or two nights at each before proceeding gradually to Jinling.
There he met Master Yanran Wei; at that time, the Elder Dajue’s reputation was as high as the heavens within the realm. That very day, the Master packed his belongings and went with him.

Just as they arrived, the Elder had returned from his travels to Daxiong Monastery. The Master requested a single room and entered the hall. The Elder hung up a plaque and posed a question, saying: "The Buddha..."

Before the supramundane path had yet emerged, he brought forth a single phrase. There was a fellow monk from the same quarters who, considering himself a leader among the assembly, said to the Master, "I shall speak with you;
let us present it face-to-face. The Master immediately took his name plaque and entered the abbot’s quarters, saying, "I present the whole dish to you, Elder.
The Elder replied, "The mountain monk is weary today. The Master bowed and stood to one side. That monk—

[The Master] said, "Heaven! Heaven! The old man said, "You hired hand! I would have beaten you right out. He then looked back at the Master and said, "This turn of phrase of yours is fit for my position as *karmadāna*.
The following day, when the summer retreat began, he immediately appointed the Master to oversee the community as the head of the assembly.

During the summer retreat, he received the most frequent blows and kicks from the Old Man (the Master). He would often say to people, "If you had not overcome your own minds to come and study with the Old Man, how could you have known there was such a thing?
This is what is meant by "Having attained awakening, one no longer sees people"—out of ten, five or six are merely fabricating it.
When the summer retreat concluded in the seventh month, he, along with nine others including Yangxi Sengong, received the transmission of the Dharma together. He resided at [Chushi].
The Master served as the second seat; from then on, he attended the Elder at his side, never for even a moment being absent.

Daily, the Elder would raise the cases of Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman and Baiyun’s entry into the millhouse to examine Wuzu. Whenever the Master offered a response, the Elder would invariably scold and revile him incessantly.
One day, raising the case again, the Elder asked the Master: "Since you have already picked it up, you must also be able to compose a verse."
[The student] said, "I have attained it; I have had an awakening. The Old Man asked, "For what reason do you say it is still 'not yet'?
The Master said, "A white tablet does not become white by itself. The Old Man said, "As for speaking, you speak well; as for seeing, you see clearly. It is simply that it is 'not yet.

The Master investigated this for many days until he suddenly beheld the countenance of the Fifth Patriarch Baizhang. He then went to report this to the Elder Dajue, saying, "This time I shall no longer deceive [you]."
"I cannot," he replied. Jue said, "I give you three more chances, and you still have not attained it. The Master said, "A great kindness is difficult to repay," and he bowed and departed.
The following day, while attending the Old Man as they were eating congee, the Old Man said, "One who understands the final phrase deserves a blow from an iron staff.
The Master said, "This old fellow has not yet even planted his feet on the ground. The Old Man—
Xuefeng said, "As expected, you cannot do without it. The Master said, "I am glad that this old man’s heels are firmly planted on the ground.
Xuefeng said, "It becomes even more unbearable. The Master then bowed. Xuefeng said, "Come after the morning gruel and receive a blow. The Master said, "The sword has long since departed.
In the winter of the year Yiwei, he traveled to Mount Tai and closed his retreat at Zibaidong Cave, remaining there for three seasons. In the year Wuxu, he returned once more to Baoyun Temple.
One day, Jue said to the Master, "The old woman of Mount Tai has been completely exposed by you.

What words should be applied here? The Master said, "A master of the school is truly not like others. Jue asked, "Where was Zhaozhou’s exposure of the old woman? The Master said, "To explain it clearly would have been inadequate.
The Master then presented a verse on examining the old woman: The old woman of Mount Tai Has been exposed by Zhaozhou. If you wish to know the reason, Look at the dog barking at the moon.
The straw dog barks at the light, revealing nothing at all; the wooden cock sings its song clearly at midnight. One tune, two tunes—no one understands them.
After the rain has passed, the autumn waters in the night pond are deep. Upon awakening, he patted the table and praised it as excellent.

In the spring of the *Xinchou* year, the Master requested leave to enter Min to bury his parents. He spent the summer at Bangkeng. While walking in meditation, he recalled Baizhang’s entrustment to Guishan regarding the "time and season."
When he reached the words, "If one arrives at its principle, it reveals itself," he suddenly lost his "cloth bag" (his conceptual grasp). Only then did he believe the words of Chan Master Dahui:
"I had eighteen great awakenings; small awakenings are beyond counting. He realized these were not words intended to deceive people; at that time, he was forty-five years old.
Later, after leaving the mountain ridges, he presented this realization to the Old Man (Linji). The Old Man said, "This accords with my 'Water Gate' on the riverbank."
The realization and the locus coincide; that is to say, by not abiding in initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti*), one darkly merges with original enlightenment (*mūlakṣānti*).

One may have attained the Chan of the Hall of Nirvāṇa, yet has not yet been able to penetrate this critical barrier. For oneself, one may achieve self-benefit; but if one acts for others, calamity arises.

At present, the Buddha-dharma is utterly decayed and rotten. To be able to penetrate this barrier is not easily found. The heavy responsibility of the Dharma-path rests upon you; take great care of yourself.
Bian addressed his入室 disciples, saying: "Xitang has returned to claim the title of 'Chanzong Champion.

You lot have fallen behind him. The Master further concealed himself in obscurity. In the summer of the Basi year of the Kangxi era, he accompanied the Elder to Mount Tianmu to reopen Shizi Zhengzong Chan Temple.
When the Elder appointed the Master to ordain monks, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Those who possess superficial knowledge or biased interpretations—how could they be fit [for this]?"
Treatise: A single awakening is the eye of rest; though my vision is now truly dim, I have not failed the old man Zhaozhou who traveled south in search of the Dharma.
His "no guest, no host" phrase shakes heaven and earth. Do you wish to know this "no guest, no host" phrase? Go ask Chief Seat Chūn in the hall.

In the autumn of the Dingwei year, by the command of the Elder [Master], I accepted the invitation from the Grand Marshal Jin Xizhai (Huzhan) and the Metropolitan Dai to reside at Ba’en Temple in Wukang.
Dharma Assembly: Entering the Monastery and Ascending the Seat. The Dragon Abyss of the Xiang Water, Mount Yu floating above; for twenty years I attended the Master’s countenance amidst ice and snow.
Without cause, I was pushed out into a mess; with shame covering my face, where can I find rest?
Although Xingchun has personally relied upon this old fellow for over twenty years, he never studied this old fellow’s Chan, nor did he ever receive this old fellow’s words.
I was simply so thoroughly scolded by that old man that my body and mind became calloused;
I was nothing but drowsy and had not yet dreamed of the Buddha-dharma. I merely remembered a few ancient kōans, which I had arranged within my belly.

Today, upon this King of Jewel Flowers throne, you have proclaimed the ancestral legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and opened wide the orthodox eye for devas and humans—unintentionally, [you have brought me to this state].
Arriving at the mouth of the wildcat cave, he let out a sneeze and forgot everything; not a single character came to mind.
He saw only the towering steepness of the Golden Wheel Peak, where ten thousand trees stood in solemn array. The mountains were green and the waters were azure; magpies chirped and insects hummed.
The autumn wind whistles; the autumn rain falls in a drizzle. What is black is black; what is white is white. The bell is the sound of the bell; the drum is the resonance of the drum.
Each and every thing is already perfected; each and every thing is luminous and wondrous. Each and every thing awakens the upward-moving faculty for you, my brothers;

Master Zhaojue Zhangxue Zuichan was the son of the Li family of Neijiang. During his infancy, he took Master Qingran of Guzishan as his teacher. His nature was serene and detached;
he remained aloof from worldly affairs (the root of entering the Way). While reading the *Lotus Sūtra*, he came across the passage:
"Even one who merely raises a hand, or perhaps slightly lowers the head, shall all attain the Buddha-way. He pondered silently: "Attaining Buddhahood is like this..."
"Is this easy? he asked, and then questioned his original teacher. The teacher was at a loss for an answer. After receiving full ordination, he traveled extensively to consult various masters.
Upon reaching Poshan, he asked a monk about Yunmen’s response to the question, "What is Buddha? to which Yunmen replied, "A dried-up shit-stick. "What is the meaning of this? he asked.

Poshan made a reclining gesture and said, "I do not study Chan; I simply love to stretch out my legs and sleep. The Master was struck with doubt and alarm, yet whether moving or still, he remained as one.

There was once a man who resembled one dead while still possessing breath. One night, he accidentally put on his sandals backward; unable to get his feet inside, he reached out his hand to pull them off.

Suddenly, he attained realization. Later, while attending Tiantong, one day as he was dragging firewood to the summit of Taibai Peak, he was wounded in the foot by a bamboo splinter, and blood spurted onto the ground.
Hearing the sound of a wooden gong echoing through the mountains and valleys, he suddenly attained great enlightenment and entered the abbot’s quarters.
He prostrated and said, "I have attained some degree of clarity. Miji made a gesture as if he had not heard clearly. The Master then sneezed.

Finally, for the sake of you brothers, he has shifted the pivotal point between past and present. He takes up his staff, disperses them, and returns to the abbot’s quarters.

Ascending the hall, he said: "Every single thing has a secret word; it is direct and goes straight to the bottom. Even if the Seven Buddhas and the Patriarchs were to come, they could not lift their two eyes.

The Master said: "A fine person is unwilling to do it; they go off instead to lie in excrement. Addressing the assembly, he said:

The Master struck him across the face with his palm. As the monk prepared to speak, the Master struck him again. The monk requested instruction, to which the Master replied, "I will tell you when the breath in your mouth ceases.
One day he asked again, "When the breath in one's mouth ceases, where does one find a place to settle and establish one's life?
The Master struck him with his whisk. As the monk prepared to speak, the Master struck him once more. The monk said, "Brother..."
The disciple did not understand. The Master said, "I rely on your not understanding. If you were to understand, even the waters of the Yellow River would have to flow backward three thousand li.
Bai Chengzhuo Chan Master was the son of the Shen family in Fengjie County. At the age of three, he understood the two dharanis of *Juntie* (Unraveling Ties) and *Jiejie* (Unraveling Knots).

Thereafter, he became extensively versed in the Five Classics, astronomy, geography, and all manner of arts and sciences. At fourteen, he entered the local academy; at sixteen, he was selected for official service.

Though his body was bound by the pursuit of fame and office, his heart remained devoted to the Buddhist scriptures. By chance, he encountered a verse from the recorded sayings of Chan Master Poshan, which read:
"I have left the household life because of birth and death; why need I further calculate the sands of the ocean? The murderous ghost of impermanence arrives suddenly;

"Carrying water and hauling firewood are known only to oneself; the wondrous functioning of spiritual powers all depends on this. Calculated, it costs nothing at all."
"Child's effort! Why must you harbor doubts in groups of three or two? The monk said, "A person who does not doubt has arrived.

Ascending the hall, he said: "It cannot be split into two; it cannot be squeezed into a ball. What is it? [Pointing to his foot,] he said:"

The Master held up a piece of firewood and showed it to him. Xiang subsequently attained realization. The Master said, "Why do you not thank me?"

A Minor Sermon by Chan Master Ji’ān of Jiangshan. The Master said: “Rolling up the curtain removes the obstruction; closing the door creates a blockage.
Yet as for this very obstruction and delusion, no one from ancient times to the present has understood them. No one has understood them! Three form a crowd; four follow in a pack.

Shai Zang ascended the hall. For forty-nine years, across more than three hundred assemblies, the Elder Śākyamuni exhausted his voice and agitated his tongue, expounding the entire Great Canon of the Teachings.
Gods, humans, dragons, ghosts, and spirits all received it upon their heads and practiced it accordingly.

But if that is not the case, you should take these old papers and wipe clean your own sores and tumors.
Furthermore, where are your sores and tumors? And how can you wipe with old paper? If you were to give rise to the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions...

If you have sores and tumors from [the realm of] humans and devas, wipe them with the old paper of samsara. If you develop sores and tumors from the three evil paths and six realms of existence, wipe them with the old paper of samsara.
If you develop sores and tumors from ignorance and afflictions, wipe them with the old paper of *tathatā* and liberation.
If you develop sores and tumors from the four fruits and four stages of the path, wipe them with the old paper of the *śrāvakas*.
If you develop a tumor of the six perfections and myriad practices, wipe it with the old paper of the Bodhisattvas.
If you develop a tumor of the burning house, wipe it with the old paper of the three vehicles. If you develop a tumor of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, wipe it with the old paper of Amitābha.
These are already proven prescriptions and medicines that match the symptoms; they have not yet emerged from the ultimate depths of the scriptural teachings.

Furthermore, there are various kinds of eccentricities, oddities, and ancient, strange growths—three types of illnesses and two kinds of lights—that one cannot escape by piercing through them nor resolve by illuminating them.

Therefore it is said: "When the wick of a lamp pricks the foot of a stone man, go at once to invite the physician Zhou; on the way, you encounter Master Pang."
I ask you all: when the sun has dried it out for six months, tell me, what do you do with it after it is dry?

*Kiṃṭha kiṃṭha saṃ, kiṃṭha hu kiṃṭha. I now release the *kiṃṭha* for you.*

A monk replied: "The moonlight blends with the clouds in white; the sound of pines carries the dew in cold. The Master [applauded].

A monk hesitated to respond. The Master then shouted. Another monk bowed and said, "I deeply appreciate this one question from the Master," and then departed.

The Master called him back and asked, "After you have received it, what is it like? The monk replied, "It is not communicated even in secret. The Master struck him, saying, "I thought you were a merchant-prince from the Southern Seas;
it turns out you are just a smuggler of salt! *Small Assembly (Xiao-chan)*: The autumn wind is clear; the autumn moon is bright. The wutong trees...
The paulownia leaves have already fallen; the vermilion cassias once more give off their fragrance. Across the vast sky, wild geese pass one after another;
in the lofty trees, cicadas chirp with a shrill cry. What need is there to speak of the ancestral intent from the West? It is far too manifest and complete.
Yang Meizhi and Guo Junjian do not rely on their own fundamental nature, but practice on a mistaken path. They come to my Xingshan Temple, morning and evening, reciting his white [mantras].

Master Yunlaozi’s "The Great Man Above" was met with a loud burst of laughter. Returning to the abbot’s quarters—Yang Meizhi [says], "The entire Tripitaka"; Guo Junjian [says], "One thousand seven hundred.

If you understand it in this way, you may satisfy the intention of Jiaguan, but you have not yet satisfied the intention of Xinyuan. But tell me, what is the intention of Xinyuan? *Heh-heh!* Evening Assembly: It has been one month since I entered the monastery.
I have been so preoccupied with worldly affairs that I have had no leisure to settle my mind on the Buddha-dharma; day after day, I have worried about rice and firewood.

The hearts of the great assembly are of one mind; they press me with such earnest urgency that it is as if I owed them a debt of money, demanding the return of both principal and interest without end.
Although Xingshan’s arms may be long and his sleeves short, tonight I cannot help but shake them out thoroughly.
Thus, lifting his sleeve and shaking it several times, he said: "O Assembly! It is better to receive little than to receive much."
To obtain a little is not as good as obtaining it now. When the year has ended and the time is exhausted, do not come knocking at doors or entering households again to demand [payment].

If you investigate and find no location, then the thought of distraction will naturally vanish. Turn back and investigate the investigating mind itself: where is the mind that is able to investigate? This is the correct approach.
"At such a time, what is to be done? One must embrace a stone and leap into the river" (only when one is personally willing does one truly encounter intimacy).
Chan Master Zhàn-ān Cháng of Jìngjū in Tāizhōu was a native of the Wú clan from Yìnní County in Sànmíng.

He received ordination under Jīnsù Wù and completed his full monastic precepts. Following Wù, he moved to Tiāntóng. Because there was a shortage of people to manufacture tiles, the Master was ordered to perform manual labor there for five years.
Each time he requested to enter the hall for formal practice, Wuzhuo said, "This matter does not depend on whether one is inside or outside; it is valued only in sincere faith.

The Master then resolved to never enter the hall again, determined instead to achieve complete penetration as an example for those remaining outside the hall. One night, while reading Wuzhuo’s *Recorded Sayings*, he read:
"Why do you not look toward where the staff points? If you suddenly understand where the staff falls, present your realization the following morning and I shall grant you my seal of approval.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "If a single word does not meet [the mark], I know you are utterly at a loss. This very moment of being at a loss is your way out.
If you attempt to seek it elsewhere, it will remain unresolved for as long as a donkey's years. My heart grows weary with age."
Gū: Who would have known that he would fall so low?
Chan Master Hongyuan of Xuedou in Mingzhou was surnamed Wang; he was of noble lineage from the Guanhai Guard of Yue.
One night, his mother dreamed that an old man led a monk into her room, and thereupon the Master was born. During his childhood, he shaved his head and donned the white robes of a novice.

He took up the inquiry, "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? and followed the Patriarch Tiantong Wuzu, yet despite diligent investigation, he did not attain realization. Later, he visited Shiqi Yun at Lingjiu.
The Master had doubts regarding Yunmen’s story of the carp in the eastern sea. One day, while attending upon Yunmen, he happened to hear a monk nearby raise this same story for questioning.
Yunmen struck him immediately. The monk asked again, and Yunmen struck him once more. When the monk asked a third time, Yunmen struck him yet again. The Master witnessed this.
Suddenly he attained great enlightenment and said, "What a pity! Those three blows were not worth a single drop. Yun said, "And what about you?
The Master shook his sleeves and said, "The heavy rain is coming! He then went out (having attained wondrous realization).
Chan Master Xingwei of Xiuhong Xiuyun Monastery in Suzhou was the son of the Gu family of Changzhou. At the age of twelve, he left home for ordination under Ven.
Benru at Xiyin Hall on Mount Huqiu. At that time, the Grand Historian Huang Shizhai of Zhangzhou, Fujian, was residing at Xiyin.

When the Master came out to receive him, his responses were so swift they did not fall into the trap of conceptualization. The Master further commanded him to compose a poem; he joined his palms and produced it immediately.

The Abbot marveled at this, saying, "This śrāmaṇera will undoubtedly cause the ancestral temple to flourish once again in the future. At twenty-five, he followed Mucun (Muxun) to visit Tiantong Wuzhuo.

Ruru Lanfangwei Jie was a native of Xi Zhou. From his childhood, he had been intent upon the Way.
One night, he dreamed of a monk wearing a *fujin* (a head-wrap) who led him to the base of a pagoda at the Three-Forked River in Yangzhou.

Seeing that the shadow of the pagoda was leaning askew, the monk commanded the layman to prop it upright. As the layman opened the pagoda door and exerted all his strength, sweat poured from his entire body. Suddenly—
He realized that body, mind, and the world were all empty. From antiquity to the present, there has been only this one self;

even this self cannot be described by name or form. He composed a verse, saying: "Within a dream, dreaming again—how perfectly real! How can listening with the ears compare to listening with the eyes?
Amidst a heap of bubbles and shadows, he grasps a precious implement; The living word of the great thousandfold world belongs to us. From this point on, he dismissed his attendants.

He observed the vegetarian fast and sought the Way with ever-increasing earnestness. One day, he visited Mucun at Helin. Mucun asked, "What is this mind that is neither born nor extinguished? The practitioner replied, "This disciple crossed the river this morning. Mucun said, "The wind and waves upon the river were fierce; how did you get across? The practitioner replied, "The tiller was in my hands. Mucun said, "Now you have already stepped onto the shore. Where is the tiller? The practitioner remained silent. Mucun struck him once and said, "If you do not speak, I shall strike you again. The practitioner suddenly attained great enlightenment. He then composed a verse: "The Great Matter is like a vast ocean;

How could there be any place for me to enter? When the wind and waves arise, I simply grasp the tiller. Now that I have reached the shore, Where is the tiller? Mucun said, "You have truly seen the Way. He then bestowed upon him the seal of transmission. Subsequently, he resided at various places such as Shuangfeng, Xuefeng, and Mount Lu. Later, he returned to the capital and stayed at the Jingshan Chan Monastery. Emperor Shenzong summoned him to the palace, where he was granted the title of "Chan Master of the Dharma Jewel" (Fobao Chanshi). In the second year of the Zhengtong era, he passed away at the age of seventy-nine.

His remains were enshrined at the Jingshan Chan Monastery. His dharma heirs included the Chan masters Foyan, Zhixian, and others. His lineage is known as the Linji school. His posthumous name was "Great Enlightenment" (Dajian). His stupa was named "Jingzhuang. His collected works comprise three volumes. He was a direct descendant of the Sixth Patriarch Huineng. His teachings emphasized the sudden awakening to the nature of mind and the practice of *wuwei* (non-action) Chan. He was renowned for his profound realization and his ability to guide disciples through his skillful means. His legacy continues to influence the Chan tradition to this day.

The Inner Struggle of the Fisherman: A Teaching for Disciples. In this degenerate age of the Final Dharma (*mofa*), those of later generations who travel as mendicants have lost their fundamental basis.

Lately, delusive and heterodox Chan has proliferated, increasingly corrupting the world and giving rise to wickedness and worldly sentiments. These practitioners borrow the remnants of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to adorn themselves;

their words are grandiose while their conduct is perverse, their appearance is that of a practitioner while their heart is not. They claim to continue the Chan of the former masters, yet they merely follow along...
They lead by following worldly conventions, causing later students to fall into confusion and ignorance.

They entice them with the good reputation of "knowledgeable ones," causing scholars to wander aimlessly toward external things and to exhaust themselves following the current. Thus they lose their fundamental root without realizing their own depravity.

All together they transmit these practices as a mark of intimacy and favor, clouding the eye of the Way and distorting the True Dharma. This is a great calamity for the Great Vehicle; it is difficult to even look upon.

They see [the truth], yet it is difficult to hear when explained; the world is unable to discern it. They bind themselves to worldly conventions to signal their own status, using the pretext of "sickness" to remain steadfast.

They employ crooked means to seek harmony, using the pretext of "constant compliance. They take up positions by twisting the straight for the sake of promotion, using the pretext of being a "master of the craft.

They bend the Way to stifle slander, using the pretext of "carefree play. They frequently associate with the common folk of the marketplace, superficially reciting the old sayings of the ancients, all while using the pretext of being "noble."

He embellishes his errors with flattery and displays his eloquence without any moral thread; his words are filthy. He claims to be widely learned, yet when at home he speaks only of poetry, and when traveling he frequents the houses of the vulgar.
Claiming to be unimpeded in wisdom, he deafens and blinds the people of the world with perverse arts while claiming to transmit the Way.
In short, whatever may serve to purchase fame or seek profit—even if they know it is not the Right Path, they do not abandon it, even though they know what the Right Path is.
Yet they cannot shoot for profit or sell their reputation; they will certainly not take [the path of truth]. Their minds are deluded within, and their forms are exhausted without.

Their cleverness is sufficient to carry this [deception], their skillfulness is sufficient to adorn it, their capacity for sophistry and analogy is sufficient to satisfy their desires, and their protection of their own influence is sufficient to rely upon for arrogance.
For this reason, they call themselves virtuous while being treacherous; they call themselves tranquil while being chaotic; they call themselves wise while being ignorant.
To claim what is heterodox as orthodox—this is the work of the swarms of externalists and the demonic craftsmen who peddle their wares.

He conversed with the Fourth Patriarch, Master Xin, and subsequently requested the Fourth Patriarch to take up residence as abbot of Laozu Temple.

He then crossed the river and reached the Wall-Facing Cliff at Shaolin. He traveled further to Youzhou and wandered through the Western Mountains, visiting the Venerable Śrī of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra at Tanzhe Temple.
After passing through Shangfang, he proceeded to Zhending to pay homage to the Great Bodhisattva. There he encountered the White-Footed Master Qidu Xian;
as the Master conversed with him, he came to understand the latter’s realization. He subsequently took him back to Huangmei to visit the Fifth Patriarch, Master Ren.

For several decades, he traveled back and forth with Dong Chan without any opposition. When the military disturbances broke out in Qi and Huang, he again went into hiding among the Red Rocks of Pujiang.
At that time, there was a monk named Lang Sheng of Dianxi, a grand-disciple of Master Ren;

he lived in solitary seclusion with perfect composure. The Master was on friendly terms with him; he once ordered a white dog to carry a letter, and Lang likewise sent inquiries via a green ape. Wei...
"From the lofty peak and the bright cliff, a white dog arrived with a letter; a green monkey returned after washing the alms bowl," and so forth.
Before long, Master Lang passed away. The Master then crossed the Tāng River and hung his rain-cloak at Yúnmén in Kuàijī.

At that time, the second year of the Xiǎnqìng era of Emperor Gāozōng of the Táng dynasty, the year being Dīngyí, the Master had already reached a thousand years of age and was seventy-two years beyond that. Suddenly, at...
On the seventh day of the seventh month, he showed his disciples, including Ruguang and Huiyun, with these verses: "Originally there is no birth or death; now I likewise manifest birth and death.
Having attained the mind that comes and goes, I shall return here again after my next life. Thereupon, he closed his eyes and entered into stillness (*śamatha*).

After seven days, he revived and instructed them, saying: "After my parinirvāṇa, you should enshrine me in a stūpa right here. If, in the future, there should be those who welcome my remains back to the West," [he should not be stopped].
"Be careful not to refuse him. Having finished speaking, he passed away. The assembly followed his final instructions and subsequently enshrined his entire body in a stupa south of the Ruoye Creek.

Whenever wind and rain occurred, the light from the stupa shone brilliantly and radiantly. In the summer of the *renxu* year, on the fifth day of the fifth month, a foreign monk arrived and circumambulated the Master’s stupa in worship;
the door of the stupa opened of its own accord, and the *śarīra* relics were vividly manifest, their brilliance beyond compare. [These were] precious bones.
He stood with reverent gravity. A brilliant red light shone forth. When the monk had finished his prayers, he lifted the cranial bone and shook it;

its joints were interconnected in a continuous sequence. He bathed it in a pond, wrapped it, and departed toward the west. A shadow drifted upon the clouds and mists, and the sound of music echoed faintly, never ceasing for days.
The Pond for Washing the Bones is located today to the left of the Śarīra Stūpa. According to records, at more than several dozen locations the Master visited, he established monasteries in each.
Only Huangmei Shuangfeng is the most preeminent of ancestral temples; because it predates the temples of the Fourth and Fifth Patriarchs, it is called the Ancestral Temple (Laozu Si).
I, Xing-sen, have the honor of residing in the master’s chamber and beholding its ancient rites, as if facing a slender bamboo by the wind.
It makes one’s five viscera grow cold within. Alas! Over the course of several millennia, how many times have the famous mountains and great rivers seen their new roofs reduced to ashes?
Yet here, these dilapidated rafters and columns continue to breathe forth clouds and swallow the moon without the slightest damage;
even the springs, rocks, pines, and bamboos still retain their lingering resonance. Could this not be due to the sublime virtue of the Master?

How could Zhong have been able to provide such divine protection? Sen once perused the *Five Lamps* (*Wudeng huiyuan*) and the *Patriarchal Successions* (*Zuochuan*), yet the records therein were somewhat cursory.

Taking advantage of the leisure time afforded by my residence in the mountains, I have conducted a detailed examination of ancient accounts of Kuaiji, including the *Tang Huisou qi*, the *Baiji leilin*, the *Luofu jiuzhi*, the *Tiantai huizuan*, the *Fayuan zhulin*, and the *Yandang ji*.
Thus, I respectfully recount the master’s life and deeds, so that his Way may be loftily suspended for future generations to reflect upon. With bowed head, I offer this humble praise.

Bearing a sorrowful vow, revealing an ancient countenance, he passed straight through ten thousand layers of barriers with a solitary staff. Upon the tip of that staff, the wind and moon differ at every ford;
beneath his feet, the mists and clouds are at leisure in every place. To express my secluded inspiration, there is only this mountain—startling the dragon back to its lair.
Dreaming of emerging by the murmuring stream; infinite meaning in the craggy stones and coiled pines. At the summit of the twin peaks, who is permitted to climb?
Addressing the assembly, he said: "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature. You practitioners of Zen:
Throughout my life, I have been foolish and vulgar, having no other interests. I alone have loved the oral lineages of the Five Houses and delighted in clarifying the words of the ancients."

My intention is not to close my eyes and deceive future worthies; rather, by nature I am indolent and unable to contort myself to seek fame, nor can I engage in the sycophancy and wit required to frequent the marketplace.
Unless one views this through the lens of the Buddha-dharma, few would fail to lose sight of it even while facing it directly.
Thus it is said: "The springtime flows on; the sun rises over the Eastern Mountain; the moon slants over the Western Brook—gaze upon Maitreya’s tower."
The Pavilion: Within the jar lies a cavernous garden, where a separate stretch of level sands unfolds. Alas for the present day; red dust and white waves stretch to the ends of the earth.

Turning my head, I see the setting sun and scattered crows. I sigh for the swallows that once pierced the curtains before the hall of Mt. Mui—where are they now? In whose home do they dwell? Addressing the Assembly:
One who acts as a teacher of the Way should be like a general facing the enemy; a monk should be like a maiden guarding her person. Take up...
If an army loses its strategic advantage, it will suffer total defeat; if a maiden loses her virtue, all matters will fall into ruin.
How can one not be cautious? Furthermore, in a letter to a friend, he wrote: "To practice Chan and study the Buddhas and Patriarchs need not be mentioned.

What is marvelous is to study the Buddhas and Patriarchs and yet be perfectly like them. Even more marvelous is that it is not only in Chan that one is perfectly like the Buddhas and Patriarchs, but also in one's character and conduct."

However, as for the Buddhas and Patriarchs, Chan is manifested from within the category of virtue; since the category of virtue is not far removed from the Buddhas and Patriarchs, what is called Chan is closely related to them.

If one studies the Buddhas and Patriarchs without knowing what this category of virtue is like, and instead seeks the Buddhas and Patriarchs through reckless words and phrases—how could such a thing ever succeed? Lately, among the so-called elder masters and great monks:

Desiring to advance forward but not being guided, I hear his voice from afar and long for him with longing. A qilin or a phoenix compared to a common deer or fowl; pearls and jade set against pebbles and stones.

The white sun casts its radiance, and the azure eyes mirror his form. Thus, one must practice a thousand melodies before knowing the essence of sound, and observe ten thousand flaws before recognizing the quality of a vessel.
Those who understand music and share the same Way rejoice together in harmony. Yet the flow of *zheng* music deludes the people.
May there be no error in my hearing. I shall briefly set forth my humble sincerity. I respectfully reply in this letter to my dhyāna-friend, saying:
I have received your letter and learned that the wealth of grain and rice at your precious monastery is piled high like mountains, and the affairs of the temple flow forth like a river.

Yet, you must bend your waist to hasten before the gates of the wealthy, lower your brow to see the patrons of the Dharma, stand with folded hands by the roadside to gaze upon their dust and bow from afar, and hold your breath beneath their carriages, not daring to raise your voice—even amidst the mud and sand. [End of excerpt]
Dust from the wind gathers on my face as I stand amidst these robes; the resolve of the patch-robed monk is thus exhausted. Facing the wind, I think of my friend, my heart knotted within.

As the former masters said, when National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang declined three imperial summons, he caused Emperor Suzong of the Tang dynasty to regard him with even greater reverence than for the Buddhas and patriarchs.
Yet, looking toward Nanyang, though our paths differ as much as clouds and mud, I turn my head to contemplate the ancients and feel ashamed.
Sweat falls like rain. How could one allow oneself to defile the Dharma-gate for the sake of a single body? The long river of ten thousand ages shall never wash away an evil reputation.
Hehe! On the tip of the fishing pole, the fisherman finds his seclusion; where there is little wind or waves, he settles his dwelling.

I laugh at that man who insists on wearing a sheepskin robe like Yan Zileng. On the summit of Laozu Peak, where the snow has cleared to reveal a pristine realm, there are only desolate cliffs, strange rocks, tall bamboos, and ancient trees.
There, one drinks bitter tea by day; rising from sleep, one drags a staff and strolls with feet unheeding of distance or nearness.
This too is a vast and genuine delight. As for debating the relative merits of "staff and shout" versus discussing Chan—this I have yet to see. Written upon the paper.

only the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of preaching the Dharma remain. I have often been burdened by this and drawn into criticism. Therefore, with courageous resolve, I have written upon the wall:
