Recalling that thirty years ago he had heard extensively of the extraordinary and magnificent scenery of the mountains in Zhejiang, in the spring of the Renchen year, he packed his satchel, took up his staff, ascended Tianfeng Peak, walked through Guoqing Temple, passed over Shiliang Bridge, waded across Xichang Pool, stayed overnight at Chicheng, and explored them all thoroughly.

At the two cliffs of Hanming, I lingered and gazed about at length. Leaning against ancient pines and reclining upon strange rocks, I frequently rubbed my belly and laughed aloud, discarding thirty pairs of straw sandals.
Then, riding the tide for two hundred li, I traveled to Yandang. Advancing toward Lao-sengya, I encountered a monstrous creature that was neither human nor non-human;
it stood naked upon the water, laughing wildly with a wind-driven madness, crying out to Heaven with a piercing shriek: "Heaven!"
Narapavata, walking through the forest without looking back, traveled for several *li*. The mountains grew increasingly deep and the rocks more secluded.
He sat down to eat at the Buddha’s Stone and rested briefly before continuing on. The stone teeth and feet were there;

majestic giant pines were present—those that curved were like parasols, those that stood upright were like banners, those that rose vertically were like men, and those that lay prostrate were like coiled dragons. Beneath the pines, the stream was deep, with a pool as turbid as stagnant mud where [the dragon] lay hidden.
He saw a wind-wheel well that resounded with a tinkling sound. Above the well, green cliffs and creeping vines were densely spread;
he entered through them windingly. At the top was a centipede, red as a *qíxīn* fish, with vermilion eyes and long claws. It lowered its head and swallowed [him], then let out a long, resonant chant.
Xing Sen subsequently spent the summer retreat at Bixiao Cave. On its left and right stood stone pillars, towering and isolated beyond measure;

above them grew *túwēi* and *cīyù* plants, such that the sun could not be seen from below. Suddenly, he heard the cry of a pheasant (*jùní*). As a woodcutter was felling timber, the resonance of the valley echoed like the sound of a lute being played.
He called out to him, attempting to converse, but the man looked back startled and fled like a deer, unable to be approached. Xing Sen then proceeded to Jingming.
The cliffs contain several hundred stone dwellings, with railings constructed along the winding rock faces. To the north of the dwellings is the "Stone of the Third Life of the Arhat.
Passing by the Great Dragon Pool, one beholds a waterfall of a thousand fathoms; atop it lies the Bathing Geese Lake, spanning a thousand *qǐng*.
As the cascade plunges into the pool, its transformations are manifold: like flying snow, like purple mist, like gathered clouds, like water-weeds, and like soaring birds.
Like running beasts, like jade pillars, like pearl curtains; sometimes scattering, sometimes gathering; sometimes manifest, sometimes hidden.

At times they produce the sound of thunder, at other times they are utterly silent. Suddenly they flash with brilliant auspicious light, and suddenly black mists close over the pool. One can never tire of beholding them; they cause one to forget the way home.
Having stayed three nights beneath the crags, he emerged from the pool to wander among the emerald peaks and the Dragon’s Nose Spring, amidst the jagged stone pinnacles.
The terrain was rugged and precipitous, like a brocade screen; the jagged peaks and crags were as dense as the shells of snails or rats. Only by winding along could one find a path.
Windows and casements faced one another, and as the mountain wind whistled through them, the bells and chimes of the halls and pavilions all rang out.

A dozen or so monks looked at one another in alarm, unaware of what realm they had entered. "Let us stop for now," they said, and all stayed overnight. It was after the full moon of the mid-autumn month.

The morning dew was clear; the mountains were empty and the moon was bright. Looking up at the stars and constellations, they all shone with great brilliance, as if one had just ascended to the heavens.
Outside the window, several hundred strange pines and a thousand bamboos rubbed against one another, their sounds scraping incessantly.
Before the cliff, the *tāla* palms stood like ghosts and demons with bristling hair. The ten or so monks looked at one another, their souls trembling, unable to sleep.
At dawn the next day, they each departed. Having returned, I still felt a lingering sense of bewilderment as if I had met them again in my dreams.

Now residing at the Double Peak (Shuangfeng) of Laozu, I often recall that journey with longing. I have specially written this to send to my fellow-minded old friend, so that the sublime scenery of Tai and Dang may appear before the meditation cushion without even moving one’s feet.
Written by the Chief Administrator (Jiansi) of Laozu, seeking a portrait of the Master.
Praise. When Xing-sen first set out on his travels as a wandering monk (*paryaṭaka*), he was stubborn and solitary, neglecting even his clothing and shoes.

Everywhere he went, many people treated him with contempt. Later, he visited the Great Master Yunmen Xue. Upon seeing him, the Master immediately granted him entry into the inner chamber and addressed him as "the eldest son of Lingnan.
He then inscribed his own portrait and showed it to him, saying: "This fellow is strange and ancient; when he sees someone who is not up to par, he scolds them with venomous abuse."
A born enemy! When he sees those who study with earnest resolve, his joy is even greater. "What are you doing sitting here this morning?

he asks—this fellow is a Zen practitioner without nostrils. How could the wind of the ancestral school ever have been silent? Upon reaching the Great Hero (Mahāvīra), the Old Man saw him and praised him.
He laughed and said, "The Great Master spent his entire life with a hard mouth, yet alas, his teeth could not keep out the wind.

He then commanded Xing-sen to lead the assembly, continuing until Kai opened Yuanzhao Monastery and took up residence at Laozu. Unwittingly, as he counted on his fingers, more than ten years have passed. Ha ha!
As for the ancestral style [of our school], it would surely be laughed at by Old Wang in a village of three households. [This concludes] the letter to the Layman Fu, written by Xing.

Sōen bows with reverence. Having heard of your reputation for a long time, I have regretted that this foolish monk, burdened by many ailments and circumstances, was unable to meet you in person to seek your instruction.

Receiving your earnest letter has greatly comforted my longing for you. Upon receiving the copy you sent of this gentleman’s compilation and carving of *nian-song* (verses on cases), I read it with increasing admiration.

However, those who "pick up" (nian) the ancient cases do so to discern the eyes of wisdom; those who compose verses (song) on the ancient cases do so to manifest the Way of the Dharma. If one picks up [the case] without correctness, the eye will be confused regarding reality.
If one composes a verse without precision, the Way will lose its authenticity. That the Way is lost stems from following personal sentiment at the expense of the Dharma;

that the eye is confused lies in abandoning what the eyes see to believe only what the ears hear. Though the ears and eyes differ, the essential principle (zongzhi) remains clearly manifest. Manifest—!
To clarify and pick out the delusive is not what can be called "picking out"; to praise the profound meaning with circuitous verses is not what can be called "praising.

If one praises with circuitous verses and picks out the delusive, then the Buddha-dharma will fall into chaos. Therefore, the essential and fundamental meaning of our predecessors must not be mixed with heterodox interpretations;
the critical discernment of the lineage of discourse must not be deceived by empty rhetoric; and the distinction between guest and host must not be obscured by deception.
Thus, when the eyes are correctly applied to the discernment of dharmas, the distinction between the true and the false is easily made;
when the clear eye examines people, the deviant and the orthodox cannot deceive it. If names and reality are inverted, one may only sigh in lamentation.

The great masters of our former school were vast and penetrating before the sound of words, their wisdom-mirror transcending the realm of thought; they were not deluded by worldly sentiments, nor did they allow names and forms to obscure their vision.
Not a speck of virtue shall go unrecorded; not a glimmer of light from a firefly shall be obscured. Hehe! The ancient path of the Yellow River flows over the golden embankments;
the new waves of green grass lap against the heavens. The village swallows and city crows remain utterly unaware; their flight and song are confined only to the earthen banks.
Because a monk from Zhejiang has come to visit these mountains, I have ventured to offer this reply. Written in haste, it cannot fully express my thoughts. In Reply to a Friend.
A letter from Gyōsen. I offer my greetings. How are the scenery and climate of Mount Hōzan? May you share the joys of the forest and springs with the various Zen practitioners?
As the seasons change between cold and warmth, I hope your daily life and health are as they should be. I pray for your myriad blessings. I trust that the affairs of the monastery do not weary you.
Gyōsen’s body and shadow lament one another; day after day I remain upon my pillow and mat, fortunately free from worldly disturbances. I have received your inquiry regarding the ancients...

Regarding the present school’s fundamental tenets: how refreshing is this lofty discourse! The fundamental tenets of the Linji Ancestor have been profound and vast through successive generations, transcending all narrow paths.
Lately, those who practice "vulgar Chan" delight in what is near and familiar, while turning their backs on what is far-reaching.

Those who wish to exhaust their hearts in the fundamental tenets of Linji are true masters; yet among people, there are also those who exhaust their hearts [in study] who may not necessarily grasp the precise intent of Linji.
To abandon this, one’s discernment is likewise slight. The spring wood grows lush and thick; I take the hand of the quail.

Though a thousand or ten thousand years have passed since the Patriarch was present, and though it has been long since we left the Patriarchs, the wailing monks of this age each recognize their own kind, and the clamorous practitioners of Chan each follow their own teacher.
How lamentable! In recent times, there has been no faith in true awakening. Long ago, Master Yuan appeared from Baiyun.
Xuedou emerged from the lineage of Zhimen; all quarters praised his diction as being like crossing the vast, surging ocean while obtaining the great power of a sturdy ship.
Thus it is said: "Those with clear vision are followed by later worthies; those with true awakening are taken as teachers by later worthies.

If one were to say that because his vernacular Chan flourished and was widely practiced, it may also be called the Way—this would be comparable to the *qin* and *se* lutes playing the music of Zheng and Wei.
Adjust it so that Kui may hear it; he will certainly not be able to call it the *Xiaoshao*.

If one speaks of "understanding Zen" as being like "genuine awakening," it is like a world entirely frozen: would a fur cloak not be warm? How warm! How warm! Yet there are still those who remain cold.
This is because they seek results where they do not belong, and practice where the Way does not lie; thus, they will certainly not arrive.
I have just met your younger brother and am delighted that his will is set upon the Way of the Buddha; I trust your uncle is taking his meals with some measure of ease.

Xing-sen bows in greeting. In reply to the Chan practitioner’s letter, he wrote: "This once-received seven-foot frame is merely a form entrusted by Heaven and Earth; it will ultimately perish along with all things.
How can you take these 'hot conditions' (the body) as something to be cherished for long? Monks of our tradition always keep their [bodies] empty."
As for the mind: one whose countenance reflects compassion does not employ worldly affectations to adorn their moral character. Regarding others, they view them as if they were sages;
regarding themselves, they view themselves as if they were insufficient. Therefore, those of the same path joyfully offer counsel without weariness.

Whether matters are great or small, they clarify them all before their eyes, and only then do they initiate and carry them out. As for what they themselves have clarified, it must never be obscured; and as for what they themselves...
This is what is obscured. Furthermore, one takes up the multitude of words; thus, the eye gains precedence over the multitude, while the multitude follows behind it.

Therefore, when the conditions for merit exceed the multitude, they are not yet worthy of esteem; when power and status exceed the multitude, they are not yet worthy of esteem; and when fame exceeds the multitude, [it is likewise not worthy of esteem].

This is not yet what is truly esteemed. What a patch-robed monk (nanseng) esteems is this: he fears that his insight into the Way (daoyan) may be insufficient, and he dreads that his lack of skill may become excessive.
He never fails to recognize what is unskillful; once recognized, he never again practices it. Now, unskillfulness is like a disease: if one attacks it, the illness departs;
if one does not attack it, it grows ever more severe. Therefore, when patch-robed monks seek one another, it is not merely for the sake of mutual pleasure; rather—
This is for the purpose of reforming what is unwholesome. If the unwholesome is not removed, the eye of the Way will not be clear; this is the natural law.

It is difficult to take pleasure in reforming one's own unwholesomeness, and it is difficult to inform the multitude of one's unwholesomeness. Only the patch-robed monk (*bhikṣu*) can do what others find difficult to do;
therefore, he is beyond the reach of the world. Having already accomplished what the world finds difficult to accomplish, he further reflects upon it.
One must drill into the core. Then, when others' admonitions are exhausted, one will fully realize that one's own conduct has been deluded and obscure.
If, while knowing one's own conduct is deluded and obscure, one cannot accept the words of others, and instead conceals one's own faults and rejects the admonitions of others—[this is a grave error].
They are but petty men. It was for this reason that the former sages were diligent in examining the multitude of worthies to observe their successes and failures.

As for those who practice deviant meditation in the secular world, they consider themselves already great, blessed, talented, and fulfilled; thus, their crimes become manifest and their foul conduct is widely proclaimed.
Those with discernment grieve in their hearts, and the sages lament in secret, yet these men never hear of it themselves, finding instead ever greater pleasure in their ways. This is so.
To acknowledge one’s own errors and the fallacies of one’s initial course—only to find that while one’s person prospers, the Way perishes—is truly lamentable.

Among the patriarchs of antiquity, there was no one who received offerings from every household or gifts from every door; yet among both monastics and laity, none failed to honor them as their ancestors. In this degenerate age, those of heterodox meditation do not fail to plunder every household and seize from every door;

yet among those with discernment, none fail to point out and condemn them. Viewed from this perspective, it is clear that among the multitude, whether wise or foolish, [the distinction between right and wrong remains evident].
To praise those who are good upon seeing them and to point out and censure those who are evil upon seeing them—this is the common sentiment of the masses;

it is not necessarily out of private affection, nor is it necessarily out of private hatred. Yet, for a monk to establish himself such that he does not praise those known by the wise, but instead points out and censures future worthies, has not yet fully realized the practice of the True Dharma.
To fully realize the practice of the True Dharma is to be like the Buddha.
This is the Patriarch’s [teaching]. Although worldly people may find it difficult to reach the level of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, how could they dare to slander it?

To stop slander, nothing is better than self-repentance; to heal defilement, nothing is better than approaching pure water. Be careful and return [to the source]. (Those who preside over the assembly when opening the hall should have this written out and hang it to the right of their seat. In response to a Zen practitioner’s letter, he wrote:
"To say that not falling into phrases of past or present is called 'seeking the extraordinary'—this leads only to the reproach of being deficient. Alas! How strange!"

Nevertheless, the patterns of tigers and leopards cannot but be extraordinary compared to those of dogs and sheep; the cries of the luan and the phoenix cannot but be extraordinary compared to those of crows and magpies;
and the radiance of gold and jade cannot but be extraordinary compared to that of tiles and iron. This is the natural order of things.
Now, what is this so-called Buddha-dharma? It encompasses heaven and earth within its true eye and subdues all categories of beings with a single pointing.
Had it not been for the shedding of the morning blossoms and the vigorous revitalization of the fundamental tenets, it would have been nothing more than vulgar Chan; of what use would it have been?
The ancient masters showed people living words, and our predecessors were intent on discarding stale expressions; they surely perceived that mere imitation and blind following were unavoidable.
It is permissible to be extraordinary for the sake of curing illness; it is not permissible to seek the extraordinary for its own sake.

Those who attempt to fathom the ocean with a shell are like the haggard woman envious of cosmetic black pigment, or the beggar mocking gold. Yet that gold and that pigment remain perfectly intact; what cause for wonder is there?
The Buddha entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa, and after twenty-eight transmissions, it reached the Middle Kingdom. From the beginning, there were no written words.

Words and phrases can be transmitted and spoken; however, one who has attained true and thorough awakening transmits and receives [the Dharma] directly. It is essential to realize this through direct penetration and resonance.
When the First Patriarch sat facing a wall for nine years, only the Second Patriarch grasped the essential meaning;

those whose faculties were slightly inferior did not belong to the true lineage. Although the monks of the present age study the "dead patterns" of the ancients, they cannot attain this essential meaning.
Even those who possess worldly wisdom and mastery of the written word may close their doors for ten years to study texts, only to carve a "Bodhi Seal" to wear upon themselves.
Thus it is said: "To embody the spirit and clarify its meaning depends on the person; if the person is not right, the Way will not manifest.
Lately, however, in the recorded sayings (*yulu*), there is a refined elegance that imitates the intent and phrasing of the ancients; their utterances are grand, profound, and strikingly beautiful.

It is certainly not lacking in such individuals; yet, when one seeks those whose vision is sharp and clear, whose essential pulse is subtle and winding—such as Master Yuan, Master Hua, or Master Baoning Yong—how can they be found in great numbers?
They truly possessed divine transformation and wondrous realization, yet were obsessed with the two characters "strange" (qi).
It cannot be fully exhausted here.
